# The hazard registry (/docs/hazards)

**What it is.** Every known way a program reading the Stellar ledger goes wrong, in 8 layers, each with its evidence.

**Why it matters.** It is the corpus's blueprint: each entry targets hazards from this list, and each hazard says which check exercises it.

[`caps/registry.json`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/caps/registry.json) is the blueprint for the corpus. Each **hazard** is a named way a reader of the Stellar ledger breaks. Some examples:

- a muxed account stored without its ID;
- a contract call that creates a trustline with no event;
- a failed transaction that still changes state;
- a valid ledger a decoder refuses.

Every hazard carries its **evidence**: an upstream issue, a protocol rule or a measurement. Every corpus entry names the hazards it targets.

| Layer | What breaks | Hazards | Covered |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | [Addresses and identities](https://xdrproof.dev/docs/hazards/layer-a) | 11 | H-A1, H-A2, H-A3, H-A4, H-A5, H-A6, H-A7, H-A8, H-A9, H-A10, H-A11 |
| B | [Values and encodings](https://xdrproof.dev/docs/hazards/layer-b) | 16 | H-B1, H-B2, H-B3, H-B4, H-B5, H-B6, H-B7, H-B9, H-B10, H-B11, H-B12, H-B13, H-B14, H-B15, H-B16 |
| C | [Transaction lifecycle and results](https://xdrproof.dev/docs/hazards/layer-c) | 19 | H-C1, H-C2, H-C3, H-C4, H-C5, H-C6, H-C7, H-C8, H-C9, H-C10, H-C11, H-C12, H-C13, H-C14, H-C15, H-C16, H-C17, H-C18, H-C19 |
| D | [State changes no operation explains](https://xdrproof.dev/docs/hazards/layer-d) | 12 | H-D1, H-D2, H-D3, H-D4, H-D5, H-D6, H-D7, H-D8, H-D9, H-D10, H-D11, H-D12 |
| E | [Events](https://xdrproof.dev/docs/hazards/layer-e) | 3 | H-E1, H-E2, H-E3 |
| F | [Ledger level](https://xdrproof.dev/docs/hazards/layer-f) | 10 | H-F1, H-F2, H-F3, H-F4, H-F5, H-F6, H-F7, H-F8, H-F9, H-F10 |
| G | [Protocol and network variants](https://xdrproof.dev/docs/hazards/layer-g) | 4 | H-G1, H-G2 |
| H | [Reader robustness (SDK-only)](https://xdrproof.dev/docs/hazards/layer-h) | 3 | – |

## How to read a hazard

| Field | What it says |
|---|---|
| `id` | `H-` + layer letter + number, e.g. `H-A3` |
| `title` | The failure, in one line |
| `evidence` | Where it was seen: issues, pull requests, protocol rules, measurements |
| `test` | What the corpus holds or will hold for it. `C5` and `S11` are classic and Soroban [recipe](/docs/corpus/recipes) ledgers; `c-base` and `s-base` name a recipe step; `M:` names a shape in the mined mainnet ledgers (`mined/index.json`); `todo` marks a placement not yet built |
| `checks` | Which check will exercise it: replay probe, conformance, linter, guide, verify facts (the guide is planned) |

The **covered** column lists the hazards an entry already targets. The rest are the corpus's to-do list, in the open.


# Layer A: Addresses and identities (/docs/hazards/layer-a)

Muxed accounts, signed-payload, hash-x and pre-auth signers, contract, liquidity-pool and claimable-balance addresses, and fee-bump sources: the places where an address is longer, or stranger, than a G key.

**Why it matters.** An address is the key an indexer files everything under. When it is longer or stranger than a G… key, rows land under the wrong account, or the insert fails.

### H-A1: Muxed account (`M…`) treated as a plain account: ID dropped, truncated, or used as identity

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, linter, replay probe.

Evidence: [wallet-backend#716](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend/issues/716) (AddressBytea truncation), #693 (two muxed over one base → PK collision), [stellar-etl#263](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/263)/#477 (fee account muxed)

Test: Muxed in every position: tx source C5, op source C5, payment dest C5, path-payment dest C14, account-merge dest C38, fee-bump fee source c-base `fee-bump-muxed-fee-source` and s-base `soroban-fee-bump-muxed-fee-source`, SAC transfer dest S11, muxed contract `W` S27; two different muxed IDs over one base account in one ledger c-base `two-muxed-ids-one-base-account-one-ledger`; muxed tx and operation sources on Soroban TTL and restore operations s-base `ttl-extend-muxed-source-text-memo`, `restore-muxed-op-source-text-memo`

### H-A2: Muxed ID extremes and non-canonical forms

In the corpus. Checks: conformance.

Evidence: [js-stellar-sdk#1785](https://github.com/stellar/js-stellar-sdk/issues/1785) (IDs that encode a different ID)

Test: IDs 0, 1, 2^63, 2^64−1 (C5 has 1, 2^63, 2^64−1; 0 in c-base `muxed-id-zero`); non-canonical strings as API vectors (exists in conformance)

### H-A3: Signed-payload signer (`P…`) stored as 32/33 bytes, payload lost, or halts ingestion

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, replay probe.

Evidence: [wallet-backend#729](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend/issues/729) (halt), #716 (33 bytes)

Test: Payload lengths 1 (c-base `signed-payload-length-1`), 3 (mined testnet 4437357), 29 (needs padding, C6), 64 (max, C6); as account signer C6 + mined mainnet `M:signed-payload-signer`; as extra signer (CAP-21) C33

### H-A4: Hash-x (`X…`) and pre-auth (`T…`) signers; pre-auth signer removed by core with no operation

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: CAP-0021/CAP-0019; removal is a state change no op explains

Test: Add both C34; pre-auth tx executes and the signer disappears C35; hash-x-signed tx C36; mainnet `M:signer-hashx-preauth`

### H-A5: Contract (`C…`), liquidity-pool (`L…`) and claimable-balance (`B…`) addresses where readers expect accounts

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, linter, replay probe.

Evidence: [wallet-backend#745](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend/issues/745) (CB/LP ScAddress as deployer), #756 (CB/LP address in event topic)

Test: Contract addresses throughout S-recipes; LP and claimable-balance addresses in classic event topics (CAP-0067); CB/LP ScAddress as deployer: s-base `deploy-from-liquidity-pool-address`, `deploy-from-claimable-balance-address` (included, trapped: the host refuses both kinds)

### H-A6: Fabricated muxed destination from a text or hash memo

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#450](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/450) (token_transfer invents muxed id=0)

Test: Memo text, hash, return and id on payments C26–C29; the memo carried into the CAP-0067 transfer event as to_muxed_id: text as a string (non-UTF-8 in C26), id as u64 (C27), hash and return both as bytes and so indistinguishable (C28, C29)

### H-A7: Forged auth entries put a transaction into an unrelated address's history

In the corpus. Checks: linter, replay probe.

Evidence: [wallet-backend#739](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend/issues/739)

Test: s-base `auth-tree-depth-245-max`: its 244 never-called sub-invocations name kits[1] 244 times in the envelope auth and 0 times in results or meta

### H-A8: Fee-bump: fee source vs inner source confusion; inner signers captured nowhere

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe, verify facts.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#464](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/464), #453, #263

Test: Fee bump success C30, inner failed C31 + mainnet `M:fee-bump-inner-failed`; muxed fee source: c-base `fee-bump-muxed-fee-source`; Soroban fee bump with a muxed fee source: s-base `soroban-fee-bump-muxed-fee-source`

### H-A9: Muxed placements missing: `Clawback.from` (MuxedAccount); muxed source and text memo on ExtendFootprintTTL/RestoreFootprint (valid; wallet-backend#753 halted on them; the JS builder refuses them)

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, replay probe.

Evidence: strkey-sep-0023.md:268; stellar-core-validation.md:217-218

Test: Clawback from M: c-base `clawback-from-muxed`; muxed tx source + text memo on EXTEND_FOOTPRINT_TTL and muxed op source + text memo on RESTORE_FOOTPRINT, envelopes built by hand: s-base `ttl-extend-muxed-source-text-memo`, `restore-muxed-op-source-text-memo`

### H-A10: Claimable-balance ID forms (union vs B strkey vs hex); derived from base account + seq + op index

In the corpus. Checks: conformance.

Evidence: strkey-sep-0023.md §2

Test: Claimable balance at op index 1, muxed op source, inside a fee bump

### H-A11: Muxed `ScAddress` rejected inside a contract-data key; events split M into `to` + `to_muxed_id` (u64, bytes or string)

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, replay probe.

Evidence: strkey-sep-0023.md:275-300; measured C26 (string), C28 (bytes)

Test: Trapped kit `put` with a muxed key (the key also sits in the footprint and the invoke arguments): s-base `kit-put-muxed-address-key-trapped`; facts on C26/C28

The hazards come straight from [`caps/registry.json`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/caps/registry.json). A tag says which check will exercise each one: **replay probe**, **conformance**, **linter**, **guide** or **verify facts**. **In the corpus** means an entry already targets it.


# Layer B: Values and encodings (/docs/hazards/layer-b)

Asset ordering, map keys that collide, amounts past 2⁵³, wide integers, invalid UTF-8, maximum lengths, nesting depth, and an authorization signed over bytes it does not contain: values that change, or break, when they are converted, decoded or verified.

**Why it matters.** A value that changes when it is converted is a wrong number in front of a user: an amount rounded, a map key lost, a signature that won't verify.

### H-B1: Asset ordering by strkey text instead of XDR bytes

In the corpus. Checks: conformance.

Evidence: [js-stellar-sdk#1766](https://github.com/stellar/js-stellar-sdk/issues/1766), [go-stellar-sdk#5974](https://github.com/stellar/go-stellar-sdk/issues/5974), StellarCN/[py-stellar-base#1246](https://github.com/StellarCN/py-stellar-base/issues/1246)

Test: API vectors (exist); a pool whose issuers sort differently by text and bytes, as a real ledger: c-base `pool-issuers-sort-differently-by-text-and-bytes`

### H-B2: ScMap keys that collide after native conversion

In the corpus. Checks: conformance.

Evidence: [js-stellar-sdk#1789](https://github.com/stellar/js-stellar-sdk/issues/1789)

Test: As value S19 (shipped), as key S20, in events, return value

### H-B3: Amounts: int64 max, precision beyond 2^53, float conversion

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#454](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/454); js #1785 (offer id > 2^53)

Test: Trustline limit i64::MAX C9/S5; balances > 2^53 stroops: c-base `create-whale-1e9-xlm`, `payment-above-2-pow-53-stroops`; offer ids above 2^53 (API vector)

### H-B4: Wide integers (u128/i128/u256/i256), timepoint, duration at extremes

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, replay probe.

Evidence: Soroban token amounts are i128 ([stellar-etl#454](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/454))

Test: Every type at min/max: s-base `scval-every-number-and-time-type`; boundaries where a signed reading of the low 64 bits goes wrong (i128 2^63, -2^63, -1; u256 2^127; timepoint 2^63): `scval-wide-integer-boundaries`; a SAC balance held by a contract above int64 max: `sac-mint-to-contract-beyond-int64`

### H-B5: Bytes that are not valid UTF-8 in "string" fields

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, guide, replay probe.

Evidence: [js-stellar-sdk#1823](https://github.com/stellar/js-stellar-sdk/issues/1823); core output becomes invalid JSON (R08)

Test: Memo text C26 + mainnet `M:memo-text-non-utf8`; ScString S28; manage-data binary C24 + mainnet; home domain and data name cannot hold non-ASCII: core requires printable ASCII (SetOptionsOpFrame.cpp:320, ManageDataOpFrame.cpp:115, util/types.cpp isStringValid)

### H-B6: Maximum lengths (VecM limits), and one past them

In the corpus. Checks: conformance.

Evidence: [rs-stellar-xdr#581](https://github.com/stellar/rs-stellar-xdr/issues/581), #598

Test: 20 signatures + 32-byte symbol S26; 64-byte data value C24; 32-byte home domain C8; 28-byte memo C26; 100 operations c-base `operations-100-muxed-ids`; max signers 20 S25; over-length as lane S (SDK only), planned in B5

### H-B7: Nesting depth: auth trees, nested ScVal; caps that fail the ledger

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, linter, replay probe.

Evidence: [wallet-backend#820](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend/issues/820); R03 depth ladders

Test: Auth depth 6 S21, 245 S22, 246 S23; nested ScVal ladder (API vectors exist); a contract deploy whose auth root carries a 245-deep chain (the walk patched for #820 runs only when an instance is created): s-base `deploy-with-auth-tree-depth-245`

### H-B8: Non-canonical encodings decoders disagree on

Not in the corpus yet. Checks: conformance.

Evidence: [rs-stellar-xdr#622](https://github.com/stellar/rs-stellar-xdr/issues/622) / [stellar-core#5509](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-core/issues/5509) (bool word 2), [js-xdr#165](https://github.com/stellar/js-xdr/issues/165) (float discriminants)

Test: Lane S synthetic vectors, SDK-only todo

### H-B9: Alphanumeric-12 asset codes; codes like "xlm"

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, replay probe.

Evidence: [js-stellar-sdk#1787](https://github.com/stellar/js-stellar-sdk/issues/1787)

Test: Alphanum-12 C9, C11, C14; mainnet `M:alphanum12-asset`; issued "xlm" code c-base `trust-issued-xlm-code`, `payment-issued-xlm-code`

### H-B10: JSON number vs string for 64-bit values

In the corpus. Checks: conformance.

Evidence: [rs-stellar-xdr#625](https://github.com/stellar/rs-stellar-xdr/issues/625); [stellar-etl#455](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/455)

Test: Covered by facts on 64-bit fields (exact strings)

### H-B11: Offer price edges: `Price{n,d}` at int32 extremes; prices as floats

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, verify facts.

Evidence: [js-stellar-sdk#1843](https://github.com/stellar/js-stellar-sdk/issues/1843)/#1750; [stellar-etl#454](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/454)

Test: manageSellOffer at n = 2^31−1/d = 1 and n = 1/d = 2^31−1

### H-B12: Maximum lengths not yet tested: `path<5>`, `claimants<10>`, `extraSigners<2>`, `dataName` 64, `operations<100>`, AllowTrust 12-char code

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, verify facts.

Evidence: RFP F14 "vectors at their maximum length"

Test: One ledger of vectors at their XDR maximum: path<5> (six offers crossed), claimants<10> with a depth-4 predicate (the core limit, CreateClaimableBalanceOpFrame.cpp:78), extraSigners<2>, 64-byte data name with a 64-byte value, AllowTrust with a 12-character code: c-base `vectors-at-maximum-length`; operations<100> alone in its ledger (the classic set holds exactly 100 operations): `operations-100-muxed-ids`

### H-B13: A valid ledger common decoders cannot read (depth)

In the corpus. Checks: conformance.

Evidence: measured: stellar-xdr-json WASM fails on S22/S23; Python 512 and Java 200 default depths

Test: planned: the S22/S23 recipe ledgers (s-base `auth-tree-depth-245-max`, `auth-tree-depth-246-trapped`) as entries in B4, expected divergences pre-registered in B5

### H-B14: Recursive delegate signatures (CAP-0071 `nestedDelegates`)

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, linter.

Evidence: cap-index.md:120; randxdr preset

Test: Custom accounts that authenticate only by delegation (kit2 __check_auth with delegate_auth): CA1 -> CA2 -> CA3 -> bob, three levels of nestedDelegates in SOROBAN_CREDENTIALS_ADDRESS_WITH_DELEGATES, payload bound to CA1: s-base `custom-account-nested-delegates`; XP002 recursive types include it

### H-B15: SorobanCredentials arms beyond ADDRESS (CAP-0071): ADDRESS_V2 binds the signature payload to the address

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, replay probe, linter.

Evidence: CAP-0071-02 (SOROBAN_CREDENTIALS_ADDRESS_V2 = 2); measured on s-base address-v2-credentials. Readers that parse credentials as source-account or ADDRESS only, or recompute the payload without the address, fail

Test: s-base `address-v2-credentials`; ADDRESS_WITH_DELEGATES in `custom-account-nested-delegates` (H-B14)

### H-B16: An auth entry's signature does not cover its own bytes: a CREATE_CONTRACT_HOST_FN authorization is signed over its V2 rendering (by design since protocol 22)

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, guide.

Evidence: By design since protocol 22: to keep one valid payload per action, the host hashes a v1 create authorization in its CREATE_CONTRACT_V2_HOST_FN rendering (maintainer reasoning in github.com/orgs/stellar/discussions/1501; CAP-0058 keeps the v1 arm usable for zero-argument creations). Code: soroban-env-host auth.rs as stellar-core v30 links it (30.0.0 @6e6c4a87 for protocol 30, 28.0.0 @ba37ea5f for protocol 28; lines 778, 803, 2641). Measured on core v30 at protocols 28 and 30, and re-checked by tools/auth-payload-check.mjs with hand-encoded preimages and node:crypto: the entry signed over its own bytes (as js-stellar-base authorizeEntry signs it) verifies only as v1 and core fails it; the entry core accepts verifies only as V2. Offline signers that sign the entry bytes, and verifiers that recompute the payload from them, get v1 creates wrong; transactions built through RPC simulation get the V2 payload.

Test: s-base `create-contract-v1-auth-signed-over-own-bytes` (fails) and `create-contract-v1-auth-signed-over-v2-rendering` (succeeds)

The hazards come straight from [`caps/registry.json`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/caps/registry.json). A tag says which check will exercise each one: **replay probe**, **conformance**, **linter**, **guide** or **verify facts**. **In the corpus** means an entry already targets it.


# Layer C: Transaction lifecycle and results (/docs/hazards/layer-c)

Failed transactions that still change state, fee bumps, sponsorship, Soroban failures, order-book matching, liquidity pools, claimable balances, and fees that differ from what was bid.

**Why it matters.** Whether a transaction succeeded, what it cost and what it changed are three different questions, and the ledger answers each in a different place.

### H-C1: Failed transactions in ledgers (fees charged, no effects, result codes)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe, verify facts.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#455](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/455)

Test: Failure suite C41–C49: one result code per tx, about 45 codes; `tx_failed` C32

### H-C2: Fee-bump inner success and failure

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe, verify facts.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#464](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/464)

Test: C30, C31, mainnet

### H-C3: Sponsorship sandwiches, revocation, `txBAD_SPONSORSHIP`

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#323](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/323) (sponsor missing in state tables)

Test: C22, C23, C40 (signer), C44 revoke signer, C45 failures, mainnet `M:sponsorship`

### H-C4: Preconditions v2 (ledger bounds, min seq, extra signers) and no preconditions

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, replay probe.

Evidence: CAP-0021

Test: C33, PRECOND_NONE C44

### H-C5: Several operations with different sources in one tx

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: participants-from-envelope rule

Test: C9 (three op sources), C22

### H-C6: Soroban failures: trapped, resource exceeded, archived entry

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#452](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/452) (`in_successful_contract_call` hard-coded true)

Test: Trapped S23; mainnet `M:soroban-failed` (3 ledgers); archived entry todo

### H-C7: Order-book matching: one op claims many offers; offers removed by crossing

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#456](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/456) (spurious offer effects)

Test: C12 (3 offers), C14, mainnet `M:offer-crosses-many`

### H-C8: Liquidity pools: deposit, withdraw, pool claim atoms, pool-share trustline without pool row

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#451](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/451), [wallet-backend#755](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend/issues/755)

Test: C13, C15, C44 (strict receive through pool), mainnet; pool-share limit-only ChangeTrust c-base `pool-share-limit-only-change-trust`

### H-C9: Claimable balances: nested predicates, claim, clawback, flags

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#441](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/441)

Test: C16–C19, C40 (expired predicate) + C45 cannot-claim, mainnet

### H-C10: Clawback and trustline authorization states (authorized, maintain-liabilities, deauthorized)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#457](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/457) (allow_trust effect types)

Test: C20, C21, allow_trust C44, mainnet `M:clawback-and-trustline-flags`; full deauthorization (authorized and maintain-liabilities both cleared): c-base `revoke-trustline-with-offers-and-pool-shares`

### H-C11: Sequence bumps and account merges (entry removed)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: 

Test: C37, C38, mainnet

### H-C12: Transaction apply order differs from transaction-set order

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: R02

Test: Multi-tx ledgers C40–C45, mainnet

### H-C13: Soroban fee charged at the maximum, refunded in `post_tx_apply_fee_processing`; `fee_charged` is net

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe, verify facts.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#453](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/453), #511; CAP-0063; measured on S10

### H-C14: Fee-bump identity: outer hash in `TransactionResultPair`, inner hash in `InnerTransactionResultPair`; inner source seq consumed even on failure, fee source seq not

### H-C16: Transaction-level failures at apply time: `txBAD_SEQ`, `txNO_ACCOUNT`, `txBAD_AUTH`, `opBAD_AUTH` (state changed earlier in the same ledger or tx)

### H-C18: Fee paid ≠ fee bid: generalized tx-set component `baseFee` (surge pricing)

In the corpus. Checks: verify facts.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#465](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/465)

Test: Classic: oversubscribed ledger with distinct bids: component baseFee 2000 against header base_fee 100, the 3000 bidder charged below its bid, the 1000 bidder applied one ledger later: c-base `surge-priced-oversubscribed`, `surge-left-over-applies-next-ledger` (equal bids are broken by a random seed, SurgePricingUtils.cpp:122). Soroban: ledgerMaxTxCount 2 with bids 3000/2000/1000: phase base_fee 2000, both kept transactions charged the same, the third one ledger later at 100: s-base `soroban-surge-priced`, `soroban-surge-left-over-applies-next-ledger`

### H-C19: An operation result whose type differs from its operation: CREATE_PASSIVE_SELL_OFFER returns a MANAGE_SELL_OFFER result

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, replay probe.

Evidence: stellar-core CreatePassiveSellOfferOpFrame.cpp:13 sets the operation body type to MANAGE_SELL_OFFER, so the OperationResult arm is manage_sell_offer; measured on c-base CREATE_PASSIVE_SELL_OFFER

Test: c-base `CREATE_PASSIVE_SELL_OFFER`: envelope create_passive_sell_offer, result arm manage_sell_offer

The hazards come straight from [`caps/registry.json`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/caps/registry.json). A tag says which check will exercise each one: **replay probe**, **conformance**, **linter**, **guide** or **verify facts**. **In the corpus** means an entry already targets it.


# Layer D: State changes no operation explains (/docs/hazards/layer-d)

Ledger entries created, updated or removed by something other than an operation that names them: trustlines from contract calls, eviction, restores, revocation.

**Why it matters.** A reader that only looks at operations misses state that changed for other reasons, and its balances drift away from the ledger.

### H-D1: Contract call creates a classic trustline (no CHANGE_TRUST, no event)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [wallet-backend#731](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend/issues/731), [stellar-etl#460](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/460)

Test: S5 (source auth), S6 (address auth), S7 (no-op on existing), P28 variants

### H-D2: XLM SAC transfer creates an account

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: CAP-0073

Test: S10

### H-D3: Pre-auth signer disappears; sponsorship moves between accounts

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: 

Test: C35, C23, C44

### H-D4: TTL extend and restore change entries with no value change

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#461](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/461) (misnamed restored-key hash)

Test: S29, S30, mainnet extend/restore; archived → restored (`LEDGER_ENTRY_RESTORED`): s-base `archival-restore-footprint`, `archival-automatic-restore-in-invoke`

### H-D5: Contract wasm upgrade, contract creation (constructor args, salt)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#462](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/462) (salt omitted)

Test: S12–S18, mainnet `M:soroban-wasm-upgrade`

### H-D6: Entries removed by no transaction: eviction (`evicted_keys`), hot archive

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: CAP-0062; [stellar-etl#461](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/461)

Test: Generated: after a config upgrade to the minimum lifetimes and an eviction scan from level 1, ledgers with no transactions carry evicted_keys: three persistent entries archived to the hot archive 10 ledgers after creation, temporary entries deleted (including older ones the scan reached): s-base `archival-empty-ledgers`; mined: pubnet 65460631 evicts 1000 contract-data entries and their 1000 TTL keys in a ledger with 162 transactions: exactly maxEntriesToArchive, which counts entries, not keys (BucketManager.cpp:1243-1268), and was 1000 on mainnet from pubnet 59516381 (mined/queries/q17_state_archival_setting.sql; at pubnet 59313516 it was briefly 0, pausing eviction)

### H-D7: Automatic restore inside InvokeHostFunction (`archivedSorobanEntries`, `SorobanTransactionDataExt.1`) vs RestoreFootprint

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: CAP-0066

Test: One ledger, two restores of evicted persistent entries: an InvokeHostFunction whose SorobanTransactionDataExt v1 marks readWrite[0] archived, giving restored then updated changes for the same key in one operation (CAP-0066), and a RestoreFootprint giving restored changes only: s-base `archival-automatic-restore-in-invoke`, `archival-restore-footprint`

### H-D8: TTL entries name data only by `sha256(LedgerKey)`

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, verify facts.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#461](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/461)

Test: Fact on S29: `key_hash = sha256(LedgerKey(...))`; conformance op `ledger_key_hash`

### H-D9: Revoking authorization removes offers and turns pool shares into new claimable balances (no create op)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [wallet-backend#817](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend/issues/817); [stellar-etl#458](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/458); [go-stellar-sdk#5974](https://github.com/stellar/go-stellar-sdk/issues/5974)

Test: The issuer fully deauthorizes mm's XPF trustline: three offers removed, two claimable balances created from redeemed pool shares (no create op), pool-share trustline removed, and the liquidity pool entry itself removed because mm was its last shareholder: c-base `revoke-trustline-with-offers-and-pool-shares`

### H-D10: Contract-data identity is (contract, key, durability); instance storage; a non-SAC `["Balance", G]` key

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#459](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/459)

Test: One contract, one key, two durabilities: (CA1, "dup", persistent) and (CA1, "dup", temporary), plus the same key in instance storage: s-base `kit2-same-key-three-durabilities`; a non-SAC contract storing a SAC-shaped ["Balance", bob] key: `kit-put-sac-shaped-balance-key`

### H-D11: External-ref executables (CAP-0085): `CONTRACT_EXECUTABLE_EXTERNAL_REF`, `SCV_EXECUTABLE_TAG`

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, replay probe.

Evidence: cap-index.md:123; [stellar-etl#470](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/470)

Test: Executable-reference entry keyed by SCV_EXECUTABLE_TAG "kit" in CA1: s-base `kit2-set-executable-ref`; CreateContractV2 with CONTRACT_EXECUTABLE_EXTERNAL_REF: `deploy-external-ref-executable`; that contract running the referenced Wasm: `invoke-external-ref-contract`

### H-D12: Frozen keys (CAP-0077): `txFROZEN_KEY_ACCESSED`, `*_TRUSTLINE_FROZEN`, offers removed

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe, verify facts.

Evidence: [wallet-backend#754](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend/issues/754) halt; cap-index.md:114

Test: CAP-0077 apply-time paths after freezing three trustlines: CLAIM_CLAIMABLE_BALANCE_TRUSTLINE_FROZEN, LIQUIDITY_POOL_DEPOSIT_TRUSTLINE_FROZEN, LIQUIDITY_POOL_WITHDRAW_TRUSTLINE_FROZEN, and a path payment that removes an offer whose seller trustline is frozen (nothing moved; the frozen trustline is still updated to release liabilities): s-base `frozen-*`. txFROZEN_KEY_ACCESSED is unreachable in a closed ledger: the check (TransactionFrame.cpp:1485) uses the same last-closed-ledger config at validation and apply, and queued transactions are re-validated after every close. Mined: pubnet 65273932, a mainnet config upgrade that freezes a fourth account

The hazards come straight from [`caps/registry.json`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/caps/registry.json). A tag says which check will exercise each one: **replay probe**, **conformance**, **linter**, **guide** or **verify facts**. **In the corpus** means an entry already targets it.


# Layer E: Events (/docs/hazards/layer-e)

Unified events (CAP-0067), event data carrying muxed IDs and deep maps, and diagnostic events emitted twice.

**Why it matters.** Events are the easiest way to follow contract activity, and the easiest to over-trust: some repeat, some carry deep data, some come from failed calls.

### H-E1: Unified events (CAP-0067): classic ops emit events; fee events before and after all txs

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#452](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/452)

Test: Every C-ledger (events counted), S-ledgers (fee events)

### H-E2: Event data carrying muxed IDs (`to_muxed_id`), maps, deep ScVal

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, replay probe.

Evidence: CAP-0067, [wallet-backend#756](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend/issues/756)

Test: S11, S19, S28, mainnet `M:soroban-event-deep-scval`

### H-E3: Diagnostic events double-emitted

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: [stellar-etl#452](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-etl/issues/452)

Test: Galexie flag profile (recipes/flags/galexie.cfg, ENABLE_SOROBAN_DIAGNOSTIC_EVENTS): each contract event appears twice, in operations[].events and again as a contract-type diagnostic event. The diagnostic core_metrics event invoke_time_nsecs is wall-clock time, so these ledgers are not byte-reproducible; the normalised form zeroes it (tools/lib.mjs normalise)

The hazards come straight from [`caps/registry.json`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/caps/registry.json). A tag says which check will exercise each one: **replay probe**, **conformance**, **linter**, **guide** or **verify facts**. **In the corpus** means an entry already targets it.


# Layer F: Ledger level (/docs/hazards/layer-f)

Upgrade ledgers, empty and very large ledgers, parallel Soroban stages, change order that varies between core processes, and the same ledger in different bytes.

**Why it matters.** Code tested on ordinary ledgers meets the unusual ones at upgrades and peaks: empty, huge, reordered or upgraded ledgers.

### H-F1: Protocol-upgrade ledgers (config settings, version, StellarValueExt)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: R02 (`'3' is not a valid StellarValueType`)

Test: Mainnet `M:protocol-upgrade` (P→current), testnet P30 upgrade; never generated (non-deterministic)

### H-F2: P30 `StellarValue` signed_ms (CAP-0088)

In the corpus. Checks: conformance.

Evidence: R01

Test: Testnet `M:protocol-30-signed-ms`; every P30 recipe ledger

### H-F3: Large ledgers (memory, many transactions)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: N4

Test: Mainnet `M:largest-ledger`

### H-F4: Empty ledgers (no transactions)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: `STELLAR_VALUE_EMPTY_TX_SET*` arms

Test: c-base `empty-ledger`; s-base `archival-empty-ledgers` (16 ledgers whose only content is eviction)

### H-F5: Parallel Soroban execution stages (several stages, several clusters)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: R08 objection 3

Test: Mined mainnet: pubnet 65485185 has 3 stages with 1, 2 and 1 clusters; pubnet 65506631 and 65517506 have 2 clusters in one stage. Generated ledgers put independent transactions in one cluster unless instruction budgets force bins apart, and equal bids make that split depend on a random tie-break (ParallelTxSetBuilder.cpp:717)

### H-F6: Change order within an operation varies between core processes

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: R09

Test: Order-variant raw bytes shipped as variants

### H-F7: `LedgerCloseMetaExt` v1 (Galexie) vs v0 (RPC) for the same ledger

In the corpus. Checks: conformance, replay probe.

Evidence: R01

Test: Every run under the base profile (LedgerCloseMetaExt v1) and the bare profile (v0); same header hash, different bytes (recipes/flags)

### H-F8: Meta version polymorphism on backfill: LCM v0/v1, TxMeta v2/v3, V0 envelopes, refunds in `txChangesAfter` (P20–22)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: ledger-close-meta.md:85-105

Test: Mined: pubnet 26588352 (P12: LedgerCloseMeta v0, 532 TransactionEnvelope V0) and pubnet 56085459 (P22: LedgerCloseMeta v1, Soroban fee refunds in txChangesAfter for 53 transactions). Every lake object inspected (protocols 12, 22 and 29) carries TransactionMeta v4, because Galexie sets BACKFILL_STELLAR_ASSET_EVENTS, which makes stellar-core emit v4 (TransactionMeta.cpp:532-536; the lake objects name stellar-core 23.0.1 as writer); a default node writes v2 before protocol 20 and v3 for 20-22, for the same ledgers

### H-F9: Same ledger, different bytes by node flags (six Galexie flags vs RPC defaults)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: ledger-close-meta.md:390-406

Test: Every run under three profiles (recipes/flags: base, galexie, bare), compared on normalised content by tools/profile-compare.mjs in make generate (recipes/<lane>/profiles/p30-mainnet.json): every ledger keeps the same header hash; bare differs from base in every ledger but the protocol-upgrade one; galexie differs from base in no classic ledger and in the 46 Soroban ledgers with contract calls (diagnostic events); variant keys carry the profile suffix

### H-F10: Config-settings upgrade ledgers (`LEDGER_UPGRADE_CONFIG`; changes in `upgradesProcessing`)

In the corpus. Checks: replay probe.

Evidence: 18 ConfigSettingEntry arms uncovered

Test: Generated: two LEDGER_UPGRADE_CONFIG ledgers whose upgradesProcessing updates contract_execution_lanes and frozen_ledger_keys, staged by kit2 as a temporary entry (Upgrades.cpp ConfigUpgradeSetFrame::makeFromKey): s-base `config-upgrade-lanes-and-freeze`, `config-upgrade-restore-and-unfreeze`; mined: pubnet 65080525, a settings vote updating 7 entries in one upgrade (including ledger_max_dependent_tx_clusters 3), and pubnet 65273932, whose upgrade grows the frozen-key list from 3 to 4 accounts

The hazards come straight from [`caps/registry.json`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/caps/registry.json). A tag says which check will exercise each one: **replay probe**, **conformance**, **linter**, **guide** or **verify facts**. **In the corpus** means an entry already targets it.


# Layer G: Protocol and network variants (/docs/hazards/layer-g)

Bytes that depend on the network passphrase, older protocols, mainnet-only code paths in core, and CAPs gated before mainnet.

**Why it matters.** The same transaction can be different bytes on another network or protocol. Code that assumes one of them breaks on the other.

Test: Documented: none reachable by a standalone P30 generator; mined mainnet entries (planned) will cover real-network behaviour

### H-G4: Gated CAPs before mainnet (`next/`)

Not in the corpus yet. Checks: verify facts.

Evidence: [stellar-xdr#317](https://github.com/stellar/stellar-xdr/issues/317); CAP-0084 slipped P28→P30

Test: `next/` channel per upgrade

The hazards come straight from [`caps/registry.json`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/caps/registry.json). # Layer H: Reader robustness (SDK-only) (/docs/hazards/layer-h)

Depth bombs, over-length vectors, truncated input and non-canonical encodings that an SDK must reject safely.

**Why it matters.** An SDK is the first thing to touch untrusted bytes. It must refuse bad input cleanly; crashing, or quietly accepting it, passes the problem on.

### H-H1: Depth bombs (nested vecs/maps past each SDK's limit)

Not in the corpus yet. Checks: conformance.

Evidence: R03 ladders

Test: API vectors (exist)

Not in the corpus yet. Checks: conformance.

Evidence: [rs-stellar-xdr#581](https://github.com/stellar/rs-stellar-xdr/issues/581)/#598

Test: Lane S vectors todo

### H-H3: Non-canonical bool/discriminants

Not in the corpus yet. Checks: conformance.

Evidence: [rs-stellar-xdr#622](https://github.com/stellar/rs-stellar-xdr/issues/622), [js-xdr#165](https://github.com/stellar/js-xdr/issues/165)

Test: Lane S todo

# Architecture (/docs/start/architecture)

**What it is.** A map of XDRProof: the corpus in the middle, the checks that prove it, and three tools that run it against real code: replay for indexers, conformance for SDKs, and a linter for indexer source.

**Why it matters.** Everything marked built here exists in the repository today and re-runs with one command, so you can check it instead of trusting it. What the grant would fund is listed separately.

![XDRProof pipeline: make the shapes, prove them, run them against code](https://xdrproof.dev/brand/pipeline-light.png)

## Built today, and what the grant funds

| Part | State | Re-run it |
|---|---|---|
| Manifest schema (JSON Schema 2020-12) with every field the RFP names | built | `make verify` |
| Hazard registry: 78 named ways readers of the ledger break, in 8 layers | built | [`caps/registry.json`](/docs/hazards) |
| Corpus: 263 entries, 634 variants, from a pinned stellar-core v30.0.0 and SDF's public data lake | built | `make verify`, `make generate` |
| Independent readers: stellar-core's own decoder and a schema walker find 737 expected values in their ledgers; `make verify` checks each at its exact field | built | `make oracle` |
| Coverage: 417 of 499 union arms reached; the other 82 each classified with a stellar-core source line | built | `make coverage-report` |
| SDK conformance runner: 6 SDK builds on the corpus and test vectors, 5 older releases on fixed-bug regressions | built | `make conformance` |
| Indexer replay harness, with a wallet-backend adapter | built | `make replay` |
| `xplint`, a Go linter for the three ingestion mistakes the RFP names | built | `make lint-selftest`, `make lint` |
| Findings reported upstream | reported | [Reported upstream](/docs/findings/reported) |

Everything above is pre-award work. The $60,000 award funds 120 engineer-days through the v1.0 release:

- the indexer-hardening guide, reviewed by a stellar-core or platform engineer;
- per-CAP and golden-agreement reports, and a memory gate on replay;
- packages for JavaScript, Go and Rust, CI workflows and a GitHub Action;
- two more indexer adapters (stellar-etl and Horizon), and runners for five more SDKs (Java, Swift, Flutter/Dart, PHP and .NET);
- this documentation site.

After v1.0, XDRProof is maintained for 18 months, outside the award budget.

## The RFP's deliverables, mapped

| The RFP asks for | XDRProof |
|---|---|
| A corpus of real and synthetic XDR shapes, each tagged with its CAP and protocol | [`entries/`](/docs/corpus) and `manifest.json`; each variant records its protocol, its source and whether it is synthetic |
| Expected decoded values for each entry | each entry's facts, every one backed by construction, a snapshot, stellar-core, the walker or review; none rests on one decoder alone |
| A coverage report per CAP and per arm | [`COVERAGE.md`](/docs/tools/coverage) per arm and per hazard today; per CAP is funded |
| Agreement with stellar-core's golden files | `make coverage-goldens` compares arm coverage today; a comparison of decoded field paths and values at a pinned core revision is funded |
| A replay harness for indexers, with bounded memory | [`replay/`](/docs/tools/replay) with a documented adapter contract; a memory gate in CI is funded |
| A linter for the three ingestion mistakes, clean on current wallet-backend | [`linter/`](/docs/tools/linter) catches all three. On unmodified wallet-backend `main` it reports 4 findings, all true, and 0 with XDRProof's two tested patches, offered upstream. Until an unmodified current revision runs clean, this check stays open |
| An indexer-hardening guide, reviewed by a core or platform engineer | funded, published only after that review |
| Findings filed upstream | [Reported upstream](/docs/findings/reported) |

## Where the ledgers come from

- **Made on a bare stellar-core.** [Recipes](/docs/corpus/recipes) drive a standalone stellar-core v30.0.0, pinned by image digest, with no peers, test-only keys committed in the recipes and no real funds. `make generate` rebuilds every run twice from scratch and checks that each pair agrees. 226 entries come from here.
- **Order is measured, not assumed.** stellar-core writes some changes in an order that varies between runs. `make order-scan` runs each recipe lane 20 times and records which ledgers vary; the corpus ships the rarer orderings as bytes, so a reader that depends on order fails.
- **Mined from the real networks.** [`mined/`](/docs/corpus/mined) keeps 37 mainnet and testnet ledgers from the public data lake, with their URLs and hashes, for shapes that are cheaper to find than to make. 36 entries come only from mined ledgers; 1 from both.

## Where "correct" comes from

Expected values never come from the SDK under test.

- `make verify` round-trips every variant, byte for byte, through native rs-stellar-xdr 30.0.0 and checks every fact.
- `make oracle` looks for each checkable value with two readers that share no code with any SDK, stellar-core's own C++ decoder and XDRProof's schema walker, and fails if either does not find it.
- `make novelty` checks that no entry is redundant: over 1,226 atoms, 182 entries hold something no other entry does, and the other 81 differ by where the hazard sits.

## Three tools that run it against real code

### Replay, for indexers

Figure: how a replay works. A corpus ledger is served by a mock stellar-rpc to a real indexer build with its own database; what it did (its cursor, its process, the rows it stored) is compared with probes derived from the same ledger, which gives a verdict: handled, dropped, mishandled, stalled, crashed or halted.

Each corpus ledger is served to a real indexer build through a mock stellar-rpc, in a fresh session with its own database. The verdict comes from what the indexer stored, never from its logs. An indexer joins with a small `adapter.toml` and a few shell commands; wallet-backend is the reference. On `main`, 618 of 634 variants are handled and 0 halt. [Replay](/docs/tools/replay)

### Conformance, for SDKs

Figure: how conformance works. The same bytes (every corpus variant, strkeys, invalid input and a depth ladder) go through each SDK build; every answer is compared with native rs-stellar-xdr (the bytes, SEP-0051 JSON, every expected fact), and the matrix marks each result pass or known (pinned with its cause).

Each SDK build is wrapped in a small program that speaks one line-delimited JSON protocol, so a new language needs one small program. Every known difference is pinned with its cause, so a new failure and a fix upstream both fail the run until the expectation is updated. [Conformance](/docs/tools/conformance)

### The linter, for indexer source

Figure: how xplint decides. A value from ScAddress.String(), which may be a muxed, contract, pool or balance address, reaches a map key that outlives the function with no check on the way: XP001/muxed-as-account. Through a switch on the address kind first, only an account reaches the sink, and nothing is reported.

`xplint` is a set of Go analyzers, one per mistake the RFP names. It writes text, JSON and SARIF for GitHub code scanning, and it fires before each upstream fix of these mistakes and goes quiet after. [Linter](/docs/tools/linter)

## Findings and disclosure

Ordinary bugs are written up and reported upstream after a duplicate search, each with a figure, a reproduction and, where possible, a tested fix. Halts and crashes anyone can trigger are reported privately first, through SDF's security channel, and are not published until a fix ships or 90 days pass.

## Distribution and CI

- **npm:** `xdrproof`, the command-line tool, and `@xdrproof/corpus`, the corpus with a loader and test helpers for Vitest and Jest.
- **Go** and **Rust:** the corpus as a Go module with a table-test helper, and a Rust loader crate.
- **Workflows** with actions pinned by SHA and a read-only token by default. `check` already runs `make verify`, `make novelty` and the linter self-test on every push and pull request; the grant adds the oracle and coverage gate to it, then conformance, replay (with the memory gate), determinism, golden agreement, an upstream watch that opens a pull request when stellar-xdr, stellar-core or an SDK tags a release, and release with checksums and provenance.
- **A GitHub Action**, `XDRProof/action`, that runs the checks on a pinned corpus in another team's CI and uploads SARIF.

## Protocol upgrades

stellar-xdr's definitions are the input. A new union arm shows up as unclassified coverage and fails `make coverage-report` until an entry or an exclusion covers it (a CI gate from Tranche 2); enum members and CAPs are counted but not yet gated. The upstream watch turns each release into a pull request with the coverage change. After v1.0, XDRProof is maintained for 18 months: new protocol shapes, issue triage, and a release for each protocol upgrade.

## Independence

The corpus, schema, tools and adapter contract are Apache-2.0 and run from a clone, with no XDRProof service in the path, so anyone can keep using them whatever happens to the maintainer. GitHub hosts the source, CI and releases; this site is generated from the repository. The tools collect no analytics. Milestone status is posted publicly in [`STATUS.md`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/STATUS.md) and weekly in #scf-general on the Stellar developer Discord.

## Security

The generator runs a standalone stellar-core (no peers) in Docker, with test-only keys committed in the recipes and no real funds or production credentials; its HTTP port is published on the host while it runs. The repository needs no secrets. Every generated ledger is reproducible from its recipe. The replay harness runs each indexer in a container with a memory limit; an indexer that is killed ends its session and is judged from its process and cursor. Halts and crashes anyone can trigger are reported privately first. The threat model, what is in place and what is still open, is on [Security](/docs/start/security).

## Technology

| Part | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Ledgers | stellar-core v30.0.0 (Docker, pinned digest), SDF's public data lake | the bytes the network writes |
| Reference decoding | rs-stellar-xdr 30.0.0 (native), stellar-core `dump-xdr` | independent of every SDK under test |
| Tooling | Node.js, Rust | the corpus tools and the native reader |
| Linter | Go, `golang.org/x/tools` | the language of wallet-backend, stellar-etl and the SDK's ingest code |
| Replay | Docker, TimescaleDB (wallet-backend's own pinned image) | each indexer in its real environment |
| Licence | Apache-2.0 | |

The same document, with more detail, is [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md) in the repository.


# Concepts (/docs/start/concepts)

**What it is.** The few words these pages use, each explained in one line.

**Why it matters.** The corpus is exact about what an entry, a variant or a fact is. Knowing these words makes every other page quicker to read.

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Entry** | One rare shape. A directory under `entries/` with an `entry.json` and one XDR file per variant, plus up to two alternate-ordering files when the change order varies. Its `id` is permanent and never reused. |
| **Catalog file** | The hand-written source of an entry, `catalog/<id>.json`: its intent and facts, addressed relative to the focus transaction. `make build` (`tools/build.mjs`) compiles it into the entry. |
| **Family** | The first part of an entry id, such as `failure`, `signer` or `archival`. The docs group entries by it. |
| **Variant** | One ledger file of an entry, for one protocol, one network passphrase and one emitter-flag profile. Its key reads like `p30-mainnet-generated`; a `-galexie` or `-bare` suffix names a non-base profile. |
| **Flag profile** | Which of stellar-core's six metadata flags a run sets: `base` (the shipped variants), `galexie` (all six, as public data lakes are written) or `bare` (none). The ledger is the same; the metadata is not. |
| **Lane** | How a variant was made: `generated` by a standalone stellar-core, `mined` from ledger history, or `synthetic` (hand-built; none yet). The recipes are also split into two lanes, classic and Soroban. |
| **Hazard** | A named way readers break, with its evidence, from `caps/registry.json`. For example, `H-A3` is a signed-payload signer stored as 33 bytes. |
| **Placement** | Where in the XDR a hazard sits in this entry. For example, `SetOptionsOp.signer.key`. |
| **Fact** | A value a correct reader must find at a JSON Pointer path in the SEP-0051 rendering, as `equals`, `length` or `some` (a matching change, in any order). |
| **Evidence** | What backs a fact: `construction`, `snapshot`, `core`, `walker` or `review`. |
| **SDK check** | A rule for an SDK helper rather than a value, such as "return all 5 entries or raise an error". |
| **Focus** | The transaction (and operation) the entry is about, so a reader knows where to look in a full ledger. |
| **Change order** | Whether stellar-core always emits the operation's changes in the same order. When it doesn't, the entry pins an order-normalised hash and lists every ordering seen. |
| **Channel** | `stable`, `next` (gated CAPs before mainnet) or `embargoed` (never committed publicly). All entries today are `stable`. |


# How it works (/docs/start/how-it-works)

**What it is.** The whole pipeline in four steps: make rare ledgers, write down what a correct reader must find, check that with independent readers, then run real indexers, SDKs and indexer code against it.

**Why it matters.** Each step is one `make` command, so any claim on this site can be re-checked.

Figure (animated): one ledger, start to finish. A recipe drives a private stellar-core, which closes a ledger; the ledger becomes a corpus entry (its exact bytes plus the answers a correct reader must find); three independent checks confirm the answers; then the same ledger is replayed into an indexer and read by every SDK build.

The full map, with every tool and its numbers:

![XDRProof pipeline: make the shapes, prove them, run them against code](https://xdrproof.dev/brand/pipeline-light.png)

## 1. Make the shapes

A **[recipe](/docs/corpus/recipes)** is a deterministic script that drives one fresh standalone stellar-core v30.0.0 over its HTTP port. The core image is pinned by digest. There is no RPC and no network (no peers); the keys are test-only, from fixed seeds, there are no real funds, and close times are fixed. Core writes every closed ledger as `LedgerCloseMeta`.

Some shapes only happen on a real network, or are worth having as real network bytes, so they are **mined** from public ledger history instead. [`mined/`](/docs/corpus/mined) holds 37 real mainnet and testnet ledgers; 37 entries are built from 22 of them, the testnet ledger where wallet-backend halted among them.

## 2. Keep the bytes, write down the truth

Each interesting ledger becomes a corpus **entry**, compiled from a hand-written [catalog file](/docs/corpus/catalog). An entry holds:
- the raw bytes;
- the CAP and the hazard it targets;
- where in the XDR the hazard sits;
- the **facts** a correct reader must find, each with what backs it.

## 3. Check the truth independently

| Check | Reader | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Byte-for-byte round trip, every fact | native rs-stellar-xdr 30.0.0; the WASM build must agree wherever it can decode | `make verify` |
| Fact values also read by | stellar-core's own `dump-xdr` (C++) and XDRProof's schema walker | `make oracle` |
| Which union arms are reached | a Python walker over the v30.0 XDR definitions | `make coverage` |
| Every arm reached by an entry, or classified with the core source line that decides it | the schema walker, per transaction | `make coverage-report` |
| No entry is redundant | leave-one-out over each entry's arms, hazards, sightings and placements | `make novelty` |

## 4. Run it against real code

| Against | How | Target |
|---|---|---|
| The SDKs | 6 builds of the JavaScript, WASM, Rust, Go and Python SDKs read every corpus variant, plus strkey, invalid-input and depth vectors; 5 older releases run the fixed-bug regressions | `make conformance` |
| An indexer | real wallet-backend builds ingest every corpus ledger, one isolated session each, through a mock stellar-rpc | `make replay` |
| Indexer source code | `xplint` follows each value from where it came from to where it is kept, for the three ingestion mistakes | `make lint` |

<Callout type="warn" title="Planned, not built">
The figure marks two pieces as planned: a GitHub Action and the hardening guide. Today every check runs as a `make` target. [Architecture](/docs/start/architecture) says what is built and what the grant funds.
</Callout>


# What XDRProof is (/docs/start)

**What it is.** A free, open test kit for any program that reads the Stellar ledger: indexers, wallets, explorers and SDKs. It holds real ledger data in its rarest valid shapes, the answers a correct program must give, and tools that check your code against them.

**Why it matters.** Most ledgers are ordinary, so the rare shapes go untested until one arrives in production, where it can stop an indexer or store a wrong balance. XDRProof lets every team meet them in a test first.

An indexer has run fine for months. Then a ledger arrives with a shape its code has never seen:

- a signer that carries a payload;
- a trustline created by a contract call, with no event;
- a map whose keys all read as "1".

Ingestion halts, or worse, it keeps going and stores something wrong. The team fixes it. Next month another team, in another language, meets the same shape.

**XDRProof turns each of those shapes into a test everyone can run.** One team's incident becomes every team's regression test, and one SDK's fix becomes a check on all of them.

Figure: the 44-byte signed-payload SignerKey from testnet ledger 4437357: type 3, a 32-byte ed25519 key, length 3, payload `de ad be`, and one byte of padding.

## One ledger, start to finish

Figure (animated): one ledger, start to finish. A recipe drives a private stellar-core, which closes a ledger; the ledger becomes a corpus entry (its exact bytes plus the answers a correct reader must find); three independent checks confirm the answers; then the same ledger is replayed into an indexer and read by every SDK build.

## What is in it

| Part | What it is | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Corpus** | 263 entries of real `LedgerCloseMeta` bytes, each tagged with its CAP, with the facts a correct reader must return | [`entries/`](/docs/corpus) |
| **Hazard registry** | 78 named ways readers break, in 8 layers, each with its evidence | [`caps/registry.json`](/docs/hazards) |
| **Schema and manifest** | JSON Schema 2020-12 for an entry; a generated index of every variant | [`schema/v1`](/docs/corpus/schema) |
| **Mined ledgers** | 37 real mainnet and testnet ledgers from the public data lake, for shapes only a real network produces, or worth having as real network bytes | [`mined/`](/docs/corpus/mined) |
| **Recipes** | Transactions for a bare standalone stellar-core that regenerate every generated variant | [`recipes/`](/docs/corpus/recipes) |
| **Tools** | Verify, oracle, coverage, generate, order scan, conformance and replay, each a `make` target | [`tools/`](/docs/tools) |
| **Linter** | `xplint`, which points at the lines of Go indexer code that make the three ingestion mistakes: 4 real findings on wallet-backend `main`, 0 with XDRProof's two patches | [`linter/`](/docs/tools/linter) |

## Check every claim yourself

The numbers on these pages come from the repository's own data or from a `make` target you can run, and each page names which. Start with [Quickstart](/docs/start/quickstart).

## What it has found

Its runs found two bugs nobody had reported. Both are filed upstream with a figure and a reproduction: [wallet-backend#834](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend/issues/834) and [js-stellar-xdr-json#67](https://github.com/stellar/js-stellar-xdr-json/issues/67). For an issue that was already open, [wallet-backend#820](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend/issues/820#issuecomment-7009772300), XDRProof offered a tested fix. See [Reported upstream](/docs/findings/reported).

<Callout type="warn" title="Not built yet">
The RFP also asks for an **indexer-hardening guide**, and XDRProof will ship as a **GitHub Action** and packages for JavaScript, Go and Rust. These are what the grant funds; see [Architecture](/docs/start/architecture). The registry already marks the hazards the guide will cover.
</Callout>

<Callout title="Early, built in public">
This repository backs a proposal to the Stellar Community Fund's RFP *XDR/CAP-Coverage Audit Tool and Indexer-Hardening Guide* (SCF #46). The corpus grows entry by entry from here. XDRProof is an independent open-source project, not affiliated with or endorsed by the Stellar Development Foundation.
</Callout>


# Quickstart (/docs/start/quickstart)

**What it is.** The shortest path from nothing to a checked corpus: clone the repository, run one command, read the result.

**Why it matters.** You don't have to trust any number on this site. `make verify` re-checks every entry on your own machine in seconds.

<Steps>
<Step>

### Get the code

```bash
git clone https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof
cd xdrproof
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Check what you have

| Target | Needs |
|---|---|
| `make verify` | Node ≥ 22.15 and Rust (cargo) |
| `make coverage` | Python 3 and Node ≥ 22.15 (`coverage-goldens` also needs git and the network) |
| `make coverage-report`, `make novelty`, `make build` | Node ≥ 22.15, npm and Rust (cargo) |
| `make oracle` | Docker, Node ≥ 22.15, npm |
| `make generate`, `make generate-quick`, `make order-scan` | Docker, Node ≥ 22.15, npm, curl, jq, perl |
| `make conformance` | Node, Rust, Docker |
| `make replay` | Docker, Node ≥ 22.15, Rust, git; the network on the first run only |
| `make lint-selftest`, `make lint` | Docker (a pinned Go image); `make lint` also Node ≥ 22.15 and git |

</Step>
<Step>

### Verify the corpus

```bash
make verify
```

The first run installs the tool dependencies (`npm ci`) and builds the native reader (`cargo build --release`), about a minute. Then it checks:

- every SEP-0023 strkey test vector;
- every entry against the schema, and its hazards against the registry;
- size and sha256;
- a decode and re-encode through **native rs-stellar-xdr 30.0.0** that must reproduce identical bytes;
- that the focus transaction is in the ledger;
- every expected fact;
- that the WASM build `@stellar/stellar-xdr-json`, wherever it can decode, renders the same JSON;
- that `manifest.json` is current;
- every [mined ledger](/docs/corpus/mined) and its findings.

</Step>
<Step>

### Go further

```bash
make oracle          # facts confirmed by core and the walker
make coverage        # the union arms the corpus reaches
make coverage-report # every arm reached, or classified
make novelty         # no entry is redundant
make generate        # rebuild every generated variant, twice
make order-scan      # which ledgers vary in change order
make conformance     # the corpus and vectors through the SDKs
make replay          # the corpus into wallet-backend, every fix
make lint-selftest   # the linter's seeded violations and mutants
make lint            # the linter on real indexer code
```

Each target has its own page under [Tools](/docs/tools). `make all` runs verify, oracle, coverage, generate, conformance, replay, lint-selftest and lint.

</Step>
</Steps>

<Callout title="Testing your own SDK or indexer?">
The steps above run XDRProof's own checks. To run the corpus in **your** test suite, lint **your** Go indexer, or replay it into **your** indexer, start at [Use it on your code](/docs/use): a copy-paste test for JavaScript, Go, Rust and Python, and the one-line linter command.
</Callout>


# Security (/docs/start/security)

**What it is.** How to report a security problem in XDRProof, how XDRProof handles the bugs it finds in other people's code, and its threat model: what it protects, and how.

**Why it matters.** Teams will use the corpus's expected values as the right answers, and run XDRProof's tools on their own machines and in their CI. Both only work if they can be trusted, so this page says what is in place today, what is planned, and what is still open.

## Report a vulnerability in XDRProof

Report it privately through GitHub: **Security → Report a vulnerability** on the [repository](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/security). Please don't open a public issue. XDRProof has one maintainer, so these are targets, not guarantees: a reply within 3 working days, and a fix or a plan within 30 days. You are credited in the release notes unless you would rather not be named.

In scope is anything in the repository that could mislead a user or harm their machine or CI: a corpus entry or expected value that is wrong; a tool, testee or adapter that runs or leaks more than it should; a workflow that exposes a secret or can be hijacked; and, once they ship, the release artifacts and packages. The policy itself is [`SECURITY.md`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

## Bugs XDRProof finds in other projects

Anything that lets someone halt or crash an indexer, an SDK or stellar-core is reported **privately first**, through the owner's security channel, and is not published until a fix ships or 90 days pass. Behaviour a project documents as by design is recorded in the findings report, not filed. Everything else is filed publicly, with a figure, a reproduction and, where possible, a tested fix: see [Reported upstream](/docs/findings/reported). The rules are in [`findings/policy.md`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/findings/policy.md).

## The threat model

What follows is read from [`THREAT-MODEL.md`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/THREAT-MODEL.md), a draft of 19 Nov 2026. Tranche 2 completes it in SDF's STRIDE template, with a data-flow diagram, a numbered threat list, verification evidence and a monitoring plan: what is watched, what triggers action, who responds and how fast.

Nothing in XDRProof runs as a hosted service. It runs on your machine or in CI: the generator is a standalone stellar-core in Docker with test-only keys and no real funds, the conformance runner executes published SDK packages, the replay harness builds and runs a real indexer in Docker, and the linter analyses other projects' Go source in a pinned container.

### What it protects

| What | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Corpus bytes and expected values | Teams use them as ground truth. A wrong value makes a correct reader look broken, or hides a real bug. |
| Pinned expectations and verdicts (`conformance/expectations/`, `replay/expectations/`, `linter/expectations.json`) | They decide whether a run is green. Tampering would hide a regression. |
| Users' machines and CI | The tools, and later the Action, run there. |
| Maintainer accounts | GitHub, npm (later), and the xdrproof.dev domain. |
| Embargoed findings | Details of halts or crashes not yet fixed upstream. |
| Accuracy of upstream reports | A wrong report costs maintainers' time and trust. |

### Where untrusted things come in

1. **Third-party code we execute:** SDK packages from npm, PyPI, crates.io and the Go proxy; indexer source from GitHub; the stellar-core and toolchain images.
2. **Imported data:** ledgers mined from SDF's public data lake.
3. **Contributions:** pull requests to this repository.
4. **CI:** GitHub-hosted runners and third-party actions.
5. **Distribution:** GitHub, GitHub Pages and DNS; later npm, the Go proxy and crates.io.

### Threats, and what stands against each

| ID | Threat | In place today | Planned |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | A wrong or tampered corpus entry or expected value | Every variant carries its sha256. `make verify` round-trips every variant through the native reader and checks every fact at its exact field; CI runs it on every push to `main` and every pull request. `make oracle` finds each value-checkable fact in stellar-core's own decoding and with an independent walker. In the last recorded run, all 49 expected 64-bit values, each changed in its last digit, were rejected by both readers. Generated entries are rebuilt from recipes. | Make the oracle's planted-value check require every value to be caught; run the oracle in CI; signed release tags and build attestations (T2) |
| T2 | Tampered expectations hiding a regression | Expectations are written from a measured run and reviewed by hand. A full replay checks a hash of the judged set, so a silently dropped variant fails the run (partial runs skip this check). | Required review on changes to `expectations/` |
| T3 | Supply chain: a compromised SDK package, toolchain image or action | Exact versions for every testee: JavaScript and Rust have committed lockfiles; Python pins exact versions (without artifact hashes); Go resolves pinned module versions at build time, with no committed lock. The stellar-core, Go toolchain and testee images are pinned by digest. Actions are pinned by commit SHA. The workflow token is read-only, and the repository has no CI secrets. GitHub's dependency graph and Dependabot alerts are on. Their first scan (19 Nov) flagged two old pins in the generator's test contract (`recipes/soroban/contract/Cargo.lock`, `soroban-sdk =25.3.0`): GHSA-x57h-xx53-v53w (medium, `stellar-xdr` ≤ 25.0.0) and GHSA-pm4j-7r4q-ccg8 (low, `soroban-env-host` < 26.0.0). That contract runs only inside the standalone generator and is never shipped; its compiled bytes are part of existing corpus ledgers, so it stays pinned. A new contract version would go out as a new recipe. Both alerts are dismissed as "not used", with this reason attached. | Hash-pinned Python installs; committed Go lock files; a review on every pin change |
| T4 | Indexer code under test misbehaving during replay | Each session runs in its own container, with a memory and swap limit, read-only mounts for the source and binary, and no secrets passed in. A process that dies or stops advancing ends its session with a verdict (crashed, or halted after one retry). | An internal network per session; a separate database per session with authentication |
| T5 | Hostile or extreme XDR crashing our own tools | The native reader decodes with a depth limit (1,500) and a 256 MiB size limit. Invalid-input vectors run in conformance (truncated values, trailing bytes, oversized lengths). | A memory gate for the replay in CI (T1); request-size limits in the mock RPC |
| T6 | Leaking an embargoed finding | [`findings/policy.md`](findings/policy.md): reported privately first, and nothing in the public repository until a fix ships or 90 days pass. | — |
| T7 | Secrets in the repository or its history | The repository needs no secrets. A `gitleaks` scan of the full history is clean. `.gitleaks.toml` allowlists three files of public test data by path (SEP-0023 vectors, strkey vectors, mined ledger index). GitHub secret scanning and push protection are on (no open alerts on 19 Nov). | — |
| T8 | Release tampering or look-alike packages | — | npm trusted publishing (no long-lived tokens) with provenance; the scoped `@xdrproof/` name; checksums and attestations on every release (T1–T2) |
| T9 | A wrong upstream report | Each report quotes only output that was run, says exactly what was measured, and comes with a one-command reproduction. So far each one was reviewed by a second reviewer and approved by the maintainer before posting; when an overstatement was found later, the posted text was corrected. | — |
| T10 | Account takeover (GitHub, npm, domain) | — | Two-factor authentication on every account, confirmed in the Tranche 2 monitoring plan |
| T11 | Expensive or abusive CI runs | Job timeouts. Only the fast checks run on pull requests. | Heavy workflows only on `main`, nightly or by label (T2) |
| T12 | Third-party code reaching the host or the repository | Testee and linter versions are pinned. | Run the JavaScript and Rust testees in containers with a clean environment; mount the repository read-only for the linter, apart from its work directory |

### Still open

- **Replay sessions are not isolated from each other or from the network.** Sessions share one Docker network and one PostgreSQL server with trust authentication, and outbound traffic is not blocked. A malicious indexer revision could read or change another session's data, which would corrupt its verdicts, or reach the internet. Today we only build pinned revisions of SDF's wallet-backend. Planned: T4 above.
- **The mock RPC listens on all interfaces** (`0.0.0.0`, a random port) during a session, and doesn't limit request size. Another machine on the local network could query it or exhaust its memory for that session. It serves only public ledger data. Planned: bind it to the Docker bridge address and cap request size.
- **JavaScript and Rust testees run on the host** with the user's environment, and **the linter mounts the repository writable**. A compromised pinned package could read the environment or write to the checkout. Planned: T12.
- **An out-of-memory kill is recorded without its peak.** The indexer's peak memory is read while it runs, so a killed container leaves only its verdict. Planned: read the peak from the kill event.
- **One maintainer.** Private vulnerability reporting is on, but there is no backup responder for security reports. Everything is reproducible from a clone, with no service in the path, and a maintenance runbook comes in Tranche 3.
- **Generated shapes** come from a standalone stellar-core, some with raised Soroban test limits. Each entry records its source and emitter flags, so no ledger is presented as public-network history unless it was mined from it.

## Status

[`STATUS.md`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/STATUS.md) is a dated public log of what has landed: reports filed, sibling sweeps, CI, and wording corrected to say exactly what was measured. Weekly updates also go to #scf-general on the Stellar developer Discord.


# Conformance (/docs/tools/conformance)

**What it is.** The same corpus bytes and test vectors, run through 6 builds of the JavaScript, WebAssembly, Rust, Go and Python SDKs, with every answer compared; 5 older releases run the fixed-bug regressions.

**Why it matters.** When two SDKs read the same bytes differently, one of them is wrong, and every app built on it inherits the mistake. This finds it first.

```bash
make conformance     # a fresh run about 2 minutes; a repeat about a second (results are cached)
```

Needs Node ≥ 22.15, Rust and Docker. Every SDK build answers the same questions about the same bytes, and the run prints one matrix: which SDK reads which ledger correctly.

Figure: how conformance works. The same bytes (every corpus variant, strkeys, invalid input and a depth ladder) go through each SDK build; every answer is compared with native rs-stellar-xdr (the bytes, SEP-0051 JSON, every expected fact), and the matrix marks each result pass or known (pinned with its cause).

A real run of `make conformance ARGS=--fresh`, recorded 24 Nov 2026:

```text
 XDRPROOF   conformance  · 6 SDK builds · 634 real ledgers

  ╭─ JS XDR-JSON 30.0.0 ──────────────────────────────── 621/634─╮
  │ ! refuses very deep auth trees                           #67 │
  │ ! accepts an invalid bool value                         #622 │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ╭─ Rust XDR 30.0.0 ─────────────────────────────────── 634/634─╮
  │ ! accepts an invalid bool value                         #622 │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ╭─ Go SDK v0.9.0 ───────────────────────────────────── 634/634─╮
  │ ! accepts an invalid strkey                            #6042 │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ╭─ Python SDK 17.0.1 ───────────────────────────────── 632/634─╮
  │ ! JSON fails on muxed contracts                          F-2 │
  │ ! drops colliding map keys                             #1250 │
  │ ! accepts an invalid bool value                        #1268 │
  │ ! accepts non-zero XDR padding                         #1262 │
  │ ! accepts a bad optional flag                          #1263 │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ╭─ No bugs ─────────────────────────────────────────── 634/634─╮
  │ ✓ JavaScript SDK 17.4.0 · Python XDR 0.2.1                   │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

 PASSED   No new bugs.   2:11

  bug status and older releases:  make conformance DETAILS=1
```

## The builds

Each build runs as a **testee**: a small process that reads one JSON request per line on stdin and answers one JSON line on stdout. The runner (`conformance/run.mjs`) judges every answer against a reference and against that build's pre-registered expectations.

| Testee | Package | Families |
|---|---|---|
| `js@17.4.0` | `@stellar/stellar-sdk` 17.4.0 (its XDR layer is `@stellar/js-xdr` 5, written in JavaScript) | all |
| `xdr-json@30.0.0` | `@stellar/stellar-xdr-json` 30.0.0, rs-stellar-xdr compiled to WASM | corpus, lane S, depth |
| `rust@30.0.0` | `stellar-xdr` 30.0.0 with `stellar-strkey` 1.0.0 | all but the native projection |
| `go@v0.9.0` | `github.com/stellar/go-stellar-sdk` v0.9.0 | all but SEP-0051 JSON and the native projection |
| `python@17.0.1` | `stellar-sdk` 17.0.1 (py-stellar-base), the current release | all |
| `python-xdr@0.2.1` | `stellar-xdr` 0.2.1 and `stellar-strkey` 0.2.0, which py-stellar-base's next major release is built on | corpus, strkey, lane S, depth |
| `js@17.2.0` · `js@17.2.1` · `js@17.3.0` · `go@v0.7.1` · `go@v0.7.2` | the releases before and after upstream fixes | sightings |

Java, Swift, Dart, PHP and .NET SDKs can join by implementing the same protocol: `hello`, `decode`, `encode_json`, `strkey_decode` and `native`. A testee answers `unsupported` for anything its SDK cannot do, and that is recorded as not applicable, not as a failure.

## What each family checks

| Family | Input | Passes when |
|---|---|---|
| `corpus` | every variant of every entry | it decodes; the re-encoding is byte-identical; where the SDK renders SEP-0051 JSON, the JSON equals rs-stellar-xdr's and every expected fact of the entry holds on it |
| `strkey` | the SEP-0023 test vectors, plus a deterministic sample of every kind of address in the corpus | valid keys decode to the right kind and payload; invalid keys are rejected |
| `lane-s` | hand-built invalid XDR: truncated, trailing bytes, a bool of 2, unknown and negative discriminants, a symbol past its maximum, non-zero padding, an optional flag of 2, a huge length with no data, a path longer than five | every invalid input is rejected; the valid controls are accepted |
| `depth` | an `ScVal` vector nested 64 to 4,000 deep | measured: the deepest value each SDK decodes, and whether anything crashes |
| `sdk-check` | each entry's `expected.sdk_checks` | the helper behaves as the check says, for example a native projection keeps every map entry or raises |
| `sightings` | `conformance/vectors/sightings.json` | the upstream fix behaves as fixed; the releases before it show the bug |
