`js@17.4.0` and `python-xdr@0.2.1` read every corpus variant exactly as rs-stellar-xdr does: the bytes, the SEP-0051 JSON and every expected fact.

## Every known failure, and why

Each build's `conformance/expectations/<testee>.json` lists every check it is known to fail, with the reason and the finding it belongs to. They are written from a measured run and reviewed by hand. After that the run must match them exactly: **an unexpected failure and an unexpected pass both fail it**, so a new bug and an upstream fix both show up.

| Builds | Checks | Why |
|---|---|---|
| go@v0.7.1 | 1 | go-stellar-sdk twin of stellar/js-stellar-sdk#1766 (Asset.LessThan by strkey text); fixed in v0.7.2 |
| go@v0.9.0 | 1 | stellar/go-stellar-sdk#6042, #6046 (open): strkey.DecodeAny accepts a claimable-balance key whose type byte is not 0 (SEP-0023 invalid vector) |
| js@17.2.0 | 1 | stellar/js-stellar-sdk#1766 (asset order by strkey text, not XDR bytes); fixed in 17.2.1 / go v0.7.2 |
| js@17.2.0 | 1 | stellar/js-stellar-sdk#1766; fixed in 17.2.1 |
| js@17.2.0, js@17.2.1 | 2 | stellar/js-stellar-sdk#1789 (scValToNative silently drops colliding map keys); fixed in 17.3.0 |
| js@17.2.0, js@17.2.1 | 2 | stellar/js-stellar-sdk#1785 (non-canonical muxed IDs accepted); fixed in 17.3.0 |
| js@17.2.0, js@17.2.1 | 6 | stellar/js-stellar-sdk#1785; fixed in 17.3.0 |
| js@17.2.0, js@17.2.1 | 2 | stellar/js-stellar-sdk#1785 (offer IDs past 2^53 rounded); fixed in 17.3.0 |
| python@17.0.1 | 4 | F-2 (findings/REPORT.md): to_json raises "Unknown SCAddress type: 5" on a CAP-0084 muxed contract address that from_xdr decodes; py-stellar-base#1234 (the protocol 30 tracking issue) asked for CAP-0084 support and warned muxed contract values would fail; this exact to_json failure is not reported; fixed on main by the stellar-xdr switch (py-stellar-base#1268; python-xdr@0.2.1 passes) |
| python@17.0.1 | 4 | StellarCN/py-stellar-base#1250 (closed): scval.to_native keeps 2 of 5 colliding map keys silently; fixed on main by the stellar-xdr switch |
| python@17.0.1 | 1 | a bool of 2 decodes as true (stellar-core's reading; rs-stellar-xdr reads false, rs-stellar-xdr#622); same class as #1262/#1263, rejected by stellar-xdr 0.2.1 on main |
| python@17.0.1 | 1 | StellarCN/py-stellar-base#1262 (closed): non-zero XDR padding accepted; fixed on main |
| python@17.0.1 | 1 | StellarCN/py-stellar-base#1263 (closed): any non-zero optional flag read as present; fixed on main |
| rust@30.0.0, xdr-json@30.0.0 | 2 | stellar/rs-stellar-xdr#622 (open): a bool of 2 decodes as false (generated.rs: b = i == 1) where stellar-core reads it as true |
| xdr-json@30.0.0 | 13 | F-1 (findings/REPORT.md): js-stellar-xdr-json hard-codes XDR_MAX_DEPTH = 500 (src/lib.rs:10, set to mirror the Soroban host's budget limit) and applies it to the whole LedgerCloseMeta, so it refuses ledgers stellar-core wrote whose auth tree is 245 levels deep. Reported as stellar/js-stellar-xdr-json#67. |

## How deep each SDK reads

Nothing crashes on the depth ladder; each SDK refuses cleanly past its limit. The deepest sampled depth each one decodes:

| Build | Deepest ScVal decoded |
|---|---|
| `go@v0.9.0` | 513 levels |
| `js@17.4.0` | 256 levels |
| `python-xdr@0.2.1` | 256 levels |
| `python@17.0.1` | 256 levels |
| `rust@30.0.0` | 256 levels |
| `xdr-json@30.0.0` | 64 levels |

A depth limit counts XDR nesting, and one `ScVal` level costs several units, so equal limits don't mean equal reach: the WASM decoder and the Python packages both use 500 and differ fourfold. The corpus has ledgers stellar-core applied whose Soroban authorization tree is 245 levels deep, and the WASM decoder refuses them (finding F-1 on [Findings](/docs/findings)).


# Coverage (/docs/tools/coverage)

**What it is.** A count of every kind of data a ledger can hold (every branch of every XDR union), and whether the corpus has a real example of each.

**Why it matters.** It turns "we test the rare cases" into a number. Every branch the corpus lacks has a written reason, with the stellar-core source line behind it.

```bash
make coverage          # arms in the corpus and the mined ledgers
make coverage-report   # writes COVERAGE.md; fails on any arm that is
                       # neither reached by an entry nor classified
make coverage-goldens  # plus core's own golden ledgers (76 MB, once)
```

A real run of `make coverage`, recorded 24 Nov 2026:

```text
 XDRPROOF   coverage  · stellar-xdr v30.0

  ╭─ Union arms ──────────────────────────────────────── 417/499─╮
  │ ✓ in the corpus entries                                  417 │
  │ ✓ in the mined pubnet ledgers                            289 │
  │ ✓ cannot appear at protocol 30, each with its reason      74 │
  │ ! need a live network: to be mined                         8 │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ╭─ Enum members ────────────────────────────────────── 333/411─╮
  │ ✓ in the corpus entries                                  333 │
  │ ✓ in the mined pubnet ledgers                            218 │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

 PASSED   Every arm is reached or explained.   6.6s

  the reasons, by kind:  make coverage DETAILS=1
```

A walker reads the rs-stellar-xdr definitions for v30.0, and lists every union arm and enum member reachable from `LedgerCloseMeta`. It then walks real ledgers and records which arms they meet.

| Ledgers | Union arms |
|---|---|
| Reachable from `LedgerCloseMeta` | **499** (and 411 enum members) |
| Entry files (698 variant files: raw `.xdr`, alternate change orderings, and `.xdr.zst` decompressed) | 417 of 499 |
| The [mined ledgers](/docs/corpus/mined) (37 files) | 289 of 499 |
| Entries and mined ledgers together | 417 of 499 |
| stellar-core's goldens (866 files, 15,306 ledgers, commit `f2b91947`) | 254 of 499 |

The corpus rows are computed from the corpus at commit <code>d505bf2</code>, the same way `make coverage` computes them. The goldens row is a fixed measurement at stellar-core commit `f2b91947`. The goldens are the ledgers stellar-core's own tests produce.

## Every arm accounted for

`make coverage` counts every arm in an entry's file, including arms from other transactions that happen to share its ledger. `make coverage-report` is stricter. An entry **reaches** an arm only when its own transaction (envelope, fee changes, apply meta) or its ledger's own shape (header, transaction-set phases, upgrades, evicted keys) contains it. Every arm no entry reaches is classified in `coverage/exclusions.json`, with the stellar-core source line that decides it. The run fails if an arm is in neither list, or in both.

| Union arms reachable from LedgerCloseMeta | Arms |
|---|---|
| Reached by an entry: its own transaction, or its ledger's header and transaction-set shape | 417 |
| `todo`: core can write it at protocol 30 and a standalone recipe can produce it; not yet in an entry | 0 |
| `network-only`: reachable in closed ledgers, but only under live-network conditions a standalone core cannot set up; to be mined | 8 |
| `historical`: only in ledgers of older protocols (range in the note) | 18 |
| `validation-only`: set only where a transaction is validated for inclusion; a closed ledger never carries it at protocol 30 | 39 |
| `not-emitted`: in the type graph, but stellar-core 30 never writes it into ledger-close meta | 17 |
| Total | 499 |

Enum members reached by an entry: 333 of 411. The report is written to [`COVERAGE.md`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/COVERAGE.md), with the entries that target each hazard.

No `todo` arm is left: every arm stellar-core can still write at protocol 30 on a standalone network is in an entry. Only the 8 `network-only` arms, which need a live network, are out of reach. A closed protocol-30 ledger never carries a `validation-only` or `not-emitted` arm, and a `historical` one appears only in ledgers of older protocols.

| `TrustLineAsset.ASSET_TYPE_NATIVE` | Core rejects native trustlines and native trustline footprint keys, so it does not write this TrustLineAsset arm into ledger-close metadata. | `src/ledger/TrustLineWrapper.cpp:84 if (asset.type() == ASSET_TYPE_NATIVE)` |


# Generate (/docs/tools/generate)

**What it is.** Rebuilds every generated ledger from scratch on fresh, offline stellar-cores, twice, and checks that the runs agree.

**Why it matters.** It proves the corpus is reproducible: nothing in it depends on our machine, our timing or our luck.

```bash
make generate        # recipes/regenerate.sh, about 10 minutes
make generate-quick  # only the two mainnet base P30 pairs, about 3 minutes
```

It needs Docker, Node ≥ 22.15, npm, curl, jq and perl, and host ports 21700–21719. The stellar-core image is pinned by digest in `recipes/core-image`, and every run refuses anything but stellar-core v30.0.0.

## The matrix

`make generate` runs **10 pairs**, which is 20 fresh standalone cores, 6 at a time. There is no RPC and no network: each core is standalone (no peers), with test-only keys committed in the recipes and no real funds.

| Lane | Protocol | Passphrase | Flag profile |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classic | P30 | mainnet, testnet | base |
| Classic | P30 | mainnet | galexie, bare |
| Soroban | P30 | mainnet, testnet | base |
| Soroban | P28 | mainnet, testnet | base |
| Soroban | P30 | mainnet | galexie, bare |

## What must hold

<Steps>
<Step>

### Each pair agrees

The two runs of a pair are compared ledger by ledger. They must be byte-identical, or identical after normalising. Normalising sorts the order of changes within an operation and zeroes the diagnostic `invoke_time_nsecs` timing value.

</Step>
<Step>

### Every shipped variant is reproduced

The list of shipped generated variants is read from `entries/` (`tools/shipped-checks.mjs`), so the testnet and protocol-28 variants are re-checked too. A full run also fails if any shipped variant was not assigned to a pair.

</Step>
<Step>

### The profiles are compared

The same recipe ledgers under the three flag profiles are compared, and the result is recorded in `recipes/<lane>/profiles/p30-mainnet.json`. Every ledger keeps the same header hash; only the metadata changes. See [Found while building](/docs/findings).

</Step>
</Steps>

It ends with `OK: every run reproduced; every shipped generated variant reproduced`.


# Tools (/docs/tools)

**What it is.** Every check XDRProof runs, each one a `make` target.

**Why it matters.** Every number on this site comes from one of these commands, and each prints its result on your machine.

| Target | What it proves | Needs | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`make verify`](/docs/tools/verify) | Strkey vectors hold. Every entry matches the schema, sizes and hashes match, and every variant round-trips byte for byte through native rs-stellar-xdr 30.0.0. The focus transaction is present, every fact holds, the WASM reader renders the same JSON wherever it can decode, and the manifest is current. Every mined ledger is verified | Node ≥ 22.15, Rust | seconds |
| [`make oracle`](/docs/tools/oracle) | Each fact's values are also read by stellar-core's own decoder and by the schema walker | Docker, Node ≥ 22.15, npm | seconds |

| [`make coverage-report`](/docs/tools/coverage#every-arm-accounted-for) | Every one of the 499 arms is reached by an entry's own transaction or ledger shape (417) or classified with the stellar-core source line that decides it (82). Writes `COVERAGE.md` | Node ≥ 22.15, Rust | seconds |
| [`make novelty`](/docs/tools/novelty) | No entry is redundant: leave-one-out over 1,226 atoms (arms, enum members, hazards, sightings, placements) | Node ≥ 22.15, Rust | seconds |
| `make coverage-goldens` | stellar-core's own 866 golden ledger files reach 254 of the 499 | Python 3, git, network | about 1 min |
| [`make generate`](/docs/tools/generate) | 20 fresh standalone cores, in pairs, across both lanes, both passphrases, P30 and P28 and three flag profiles. Every pair agrees, and every shipped generated variant is reproduced | Docker, Node, npm, curl, jq, perl | about 10 min |
| `make generate-quick` | The two mainnet base P30 pairs only | the same | about 3 min |
| [`make order-scan`](/docs/tools/order-scan) | 20 fresh runs per lane: which ledgers vary in change order; content never does | Docker | about 15 min |
| [`make conformance`](/docs/tools/conformance) | Every corpus variant, the strkeys, the invalid-input vectors and a depth ladder go through 6 SDK builds; 5 older releases run the fixed-bug regressions. js-stellar-sdk 17.4.0 and `stellar-xdr` 0.2.1 read every variant exactly as rs-stellar-xdr does; every other difference is pinned with its cause | Node, Rust, Docker | about 2 min warm |
| [`make replay`](/docs/tools/replay) | The whole corpus into wallet-backend `main` (618 of 634 handled, 0 halted), and every fixed failure before and after its fix. Every verdict is pinned | Docker, Node ≥ 22.15, Rust, git | about 20 min cold |
| [`make lint-selftest`](/docs/tools/linter#self-test) | The linter catches all 44 seeded violations and all 17 mutants, and flags none of 31 good cases | Docker | about 2 min warm |
| [`make lint`](/docs/tools/linter) | The linter on real code: wallet-backend `main` (4 findings, all true; 0 with the two patches), stellar-etl (12), go-stellar-sdk ingest (0), the commits around upstream fixes and fixed bugs put back. Every finding is pinned and triaged | Docker, Node ≥ 22.15, git | about 3 min warm |

`make all` runs verify, oracle, coverage, generate, conformance, replay, lint-selftest and lint.

`make build` is not a check: it compiles `catalog/` into `entries/` from the runs of `make generate` and `mined/`, in minutes. See [Catalog](/docs/corpus/catalog).

## The readers behind them

| Reader | What it is | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| Native reader | A small Rust program on `stellar-xdr` 30.0.0 (depth limit 1500) that decodes, renders SEP-0051 JSON and re-encodes | verify, novelty, coverage-report, conformance (the reference), replay |
| WASM reader | `@stellar/stellar-xdr-json` 30.0.0, a second opinion | verify, conformance |
| `stellar-core` | Core's own C++ `dump-xdr`, in Docker with no network, on the pinned image | oracle |
| Schema walker | `walker.mjs`: XDRProof's own JavaScript reader, driven only by the XDR definitions; it shares no code with any SDK | oracle |
| Coverage walker | `xdrcov.py`: a Python walker over the same v30.0 definitions that records every union arm and enum member it meets | coverage |
| xplint | Go analyzers over SSA (`golang.org/x/tools`), built and run in a pinned Go image | lint, lint-selftest |
| Segment walker | the schema walker again, attributing every arm it meets to the transaction envelope or result meta it sits in, or to the ledger itself | coverage-report, novelty |


# Linter (/docs/tools/linter)

**What it is.** `xplint` reads the Go source of an indexer and points at the lines that make one of three mistakes: trusting a field stellar-core never checked, walking a nested structure with no limit, or taking a transaction's participants from what it asked for instead of what happened.

**Why it matters.** These three mistakes are how real indexers have halted or stored wrong data. The linter finds the code patterns themselves, whether or not a ledger has triggered them yet. On wallet-backend `main` it reports 4, all real code patterns and none reachable by a ledger today: one is hardening at today's limits, three sit in code Blend's contracts cannot reach. With XDRProof's two patches it reports 0.

![A terminal: xplint on wallet-backend main reports four findings (one unbounded walk, three muxed addresses used as accounts), writes the same four as SARIF, then both XDRProof patches are applied and xplint exits 0 with no findings.](https://xdrproof.dev/gifs/lint.gif)

## Run it

```bash
go install github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/linter/cmd/xplint@main
xplint ./...                               # text, one finding a line
xplint -format sarif -o xplint.sarif ./... # GitHub code scanning
xplint -format json ./...
xplint -rules XP002,XP003/declared-auth ./...
xplint -list                               # every rule, with evidence
```

The exit status is 0 with no findings, 1 with findings, and 2 when the packages could not be loaded. It needs the same Go toolchain and cgo setup the packages build with.

In this repository, both targets run in a pinned Go image (`linter/toolchain-image`) through `linter/go.sh`:

```bash
make lint-selftest   # seeded fixtures and mutants (~2 min warm)
make lint            # real code, against expectations.json (about 8 min fresh; seconds when nothing changed)
```

## The three mistakes

3 rules, 12 sub-rules on by default (13 in all). Each sub-rule has a stable ID, used as the SARIF `ruleId`. The table is read from `linter/xplint/rules.go`.

| Sub-rule | Level | Flags | Instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| `XP001/text-bytes` | warning | Memo text, ScString and ScSymbol are raw bytes stellar-core does not check; this value reaches storage or a JSON encoder unchecked | Check utf8.ValidString (and reject NUL) before storing or encoding, or store the bytes as hex or base64. |
| `XP001/muxed-as-account` | error | A muxed address (M..., or any ScAddress kind) is used where an account is expected | Use ToAccountId().Address() for the account and keep the muxed ID in its own field; switch on ScAddress.Type before treating it as an account. |
| `XP001/mux-id-as-identity` | warning | A muxed ID is read with its error ignored, or narrowed to a signed or floating type | Check the error from GetId (a plain G account has no ID) and keep the ID as uint64 or a decimal string; core does not validate it. |
| `XP001/contract-number` | warning | An integer chosen by a contract (an ScVal) sizes an allocation, an exponent or a shift without a bound | Compare it against a constant limit before using it as an exponent, size or shift count. |
| `XP001/declared-footprint` | warning | The Soroban footprint is what the submitter declared; it is used here as the contract or entries the transaction touched | Read the contract from the operation's ledger entry changes or events, or confirm the declared one against them. |
| `XP002/walk-unbudgeted` | warning | A recursive walk over a self-referential XDR type has no depth or node budget; nesting is chosen by the submitter | Carry a depth counter and a node count; when a limit is reached, stop descending and continue (log or count it). Never fail the ledger. |
| `XP002/budget-fails` | error | A recursive walk returns an error when its depth or node budget is exceeded; the error repeats on every retry and halts ingestion | Stop descending and continue (log or count it). Core can close a ledger with a larger tree than any limit the indexer picks. |
| `XP002/decode-unlimited` | error | XDR is decoded with no depth limit, or a limit above the SDK default | Decode with the default limit (xdr.SafeUnmarshal, MaxDepth 1500) or lower. |
| `XP002/alloc-from-wire` | warning | An allocation is sized from an integer read off the wire, with no bound | Bound the size against a constant before allocating. |
| `XP002/implicit-walk` | note, off by default | An SDK helper (String, Equals, fmt %v) recurses over a submitter-nested value with no budget of its own | It is bounded only by the decoder's depth limit; avoid it on hot paths or on values whose depth you have not bounded. |
| `XP003/declared-auth` | error | An address from the declared Soroban authorization tree is attributed without confirmation from the meta | An auth entry says what was permitted, not what ran. Take the address from nonce entries, ledger entry changes or events, or confirm it against them. |
| `XP003/op-body-ungated` | warning | An account from an operation body is attributed with no check that the transaction succeeded | A failed transaction changes nothing but its fee. Attribute operation-body accounts only when the transaction succeeded. |
| `XP003/events-ungated` | warning | Diagnostic events are used for attribution with no check that the transaction succeeded | Diagnostic events exist for failed transactions; InSuccessfulContractCall is per call, not per transaction. |

## How it decides

Figure: how xplint decides. A value from ScAddress.String(), which may be a muxed, contract, pool or balance address, reaches a map key that outlives the function with no check on the way: XP001/muxed-as-account. Through a switch on the address kind first, only an account reaches the sink, and nothing is reported.

- **Where a value came from.** Each value carries labels for its source: text bytes, a possibly muxed address, a number a contract chose, the declared footprint, the authorization tree, an operation body, a diagnostic event. Sources are named SDK calls, conversions and field reads.
- **Where it is kept.** A sink is where a value is stored: a JSON- or db-tagged field, a map key, a set member, a builder's account. A map or set counts only when it outlives the function; a scratch map for de-duplication is not attribution.
- **What clears it.** A check counts only when every path to the sink passes through it, and only for the value it checked: checking `good` does not clear `bad + good`. A success check clears operation bodies and events on its branch.
- **Recursion.** XP002 finds recursive walks over the XDR types that can nest, computed from the SDK's own type graph, so CAP-0071's nested delegates are covered without a list. A budget must stop the walk; a budget that only logs, or that fails the ledger, is reported.

## Self-test

`make lint-selftest` runs xplint on seeded fixtures, each modelled on real code and named in its fixture, then mutates the good cases.

44 seeded violations, each caught at its marked line · 31 good cases, none flagged · 17 mutants of the good cases, each caught

The near misses are seeded too: a check on a different memo than the one stored, a bound on the wrong branch, `max` used as a bound, a helper that calls the UTF-8 check and ignores it, a budget that only logs, a method that happens to be called `Successful`.

## Limits

- Calls through interfaces and function values are not followed (closures are), nor values sent over channels.
- Flows through a database are not followed: wallet-backend #802 (Blend decimals stored, read back and used as an exponent) is out of reach; the in-memory shape is caught.
- Memory is tracked one struct field deep; deeper fields and slice elements share their root's labels.
- The sources and sinks are a catalogue of go-stellar-sdk and standard-library calls (`xplint/sdk.go`); code that reads XDR through its own types needs entries added.
- No false-positive rate is claimed. Every finding on the three codebases and on the history commits is triaged true, but three codebases are too few to state a rate.

The full list is in [`linter/README.md`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/linter/README.md).


# Novelty (/docs/tools/novelty)

**What it is.** A check that every entry earns its place: each must hold something no other entry holds.

**Why it matters.** The corpus grows by purpose, not by volume, so a team can run all of it without wading through duplicates.

```bash
make novelty                    # node tools/novelty.mjs
node tools/novelty.mjs --json out.json   # also write the per-entry report
```

The corpus grows by purpose, not volume. Novelty checks that every entry earns its place. It describes each entry as a set of **atoms**:

| Atom | What counts |
|---|---|
| Union arms and enum members | those reached by the entry's own transaction (its envelope and result meta) or by its ledger's own shape (header, transaction-set phases, upgrades, evicted keys), in any variant. Other transactions that share the ledger count for nothing |
| Hazards | each hazard the entry targets |
| Sightings | each upstream issue it reproduces |
| Placements | each pair of a hazard and where in the XDR it sits |

An entry is **redundant** when every one of its atoms is also held by some other entry. Each entry is left out in turn, so the result does not depend on the order entries are read, unlike a greedy "does it add anything new" pass. The run exits 1 if any entry is redundant.

## Today

At commit <code>d505bf2</code>: 0 redundant entries, over 1,226 atoms.

| Entries | Count |
|---|---:|
| Hold an arm, enum member, hazard or sighting no other entry holds | 182 |
| Told apart only by a placement | 81 |
| … of which every other atom sits inside one single other entry | 11 |

<Callout title="Placement is a claim, not a measurement">A placement is text the author wrote. So `make novelty` lists every entry told apart only by placement, and flags the ones wholly contained in one other entry: for each such pair, the facts must check a different thing.</Callout>

It needs Node ≥ 22.15 and the native reader (Rust), which finds each variant's transaction hashes.


# Oracle (/docs/tools/oracle)

**What it is.** A second and a third opinion on every expected value, from two readers that share no code with any SDK: stellar-core's own decoder and XDRProof's own walker.

**Why it matters.** A test is only as good as its expected answer. Readers that cannot share a bug with the SDK under test keep the answers honest.

```bash
make oracle          # node tools/oracle.mjs
node tools/oracle.mjs --write  # also writes the evidence into entries
```

A fact is only as good as the reader that produced it. The oracle asks two readers that share no code with any SDK:

| Reader | How it runs |
|---|---|
| **stellar-core** | `stellar-core dump-xdr`, inside `docker run --network none` on the `stellar/quickstart` image pinned by digest in `recipes/core-image` (override with `XDRPROOF_CORE_IMAGE`) |
| **Schema walker** | `tools/walker.mjs`, driven only by the v30.0 XDR definitions. It rejects non-zero padding, over-length values, bad enums and trailing bytes |

For each fact, the oracle takes its expected values and checks that they appear among the values each reader produced. Enum values are checked too: `tools/coverage/defs/sep0051-enum-names.json` maps every XDR enum member to the string SEP-0051 prints for it, so the walker confirms a member it reached and stellar-core one its dump printed. Enum names are matched by name across all enums, anywhere in the ledger, so a common name such as `success` is a weak confirmation. A `length` fact has no value to check, and a `v0`-style arm name is structure, not a value. A value either reader misses is a **disagreement**, and the run fails. So does a ledger stellar-core cannot print: nothing in it is confirmed. With `--write`, it records `core` and `walker` in the fact's evidence.

## A planted error must be caught

A reader that finds every value might simply accept anything. So the oracle tests itself. It takes every expected value of 10 or more digits (64-bit amounts, IDs and fees), changes its last digit and asks both readers again.

| Result | Counts as |
|---|---|
| Both readers reject the changed value | caught |
| Both readers find it: the changed value occurs elsewhere in the same ledger | a coincidence, not a failure |
| Only one reader finds it | a **disagreement**: the run fails |

If no planted error is caught at all, the self-test fails and the run exits 1.

<Callout title="What it does not check">It checks that a value is present in a reader's output, not that it sits at the fact's path; the path is checked by [Verify](/docs/tools/verify).</Callout>


# Order scan (/docs/tools/order-scan)

**What it is.** A measurement of how often stellar-core writes the same ledger's changes in a different order.

**Why it matters.** Code that assumes a fixed order works on one run and breaks on the next. The corpus ships the rarer orderings, so that code fails in a test instead.

```bash
make order-scan   # 20 runs per lane, classic then Soroban (~15 min)
```

stellar-core iterates a hash map with a per-process random salt, so the changes within an operation can come out in a different order on every run. The order scan measures this. It runs each recipe lane 20 times on fresh cores, records every byte ordering seen per ledger, and fails if any ledger's **content** differs once order is normalised.

## The committed results

Results are in `recipes/classic/order-scan/p30-mainnet-base.json` and `recipes/soroban/order-scan/p30-mainnet-base.json`:

| Lane | Runs | Ledgers that vary in order | Content that varies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classic | 20 | 33 of 103 recipe ledgers; 12, 14, 78, 80, 84 differ in every run | 0 |
| Soroban | 20 | 16 of 92 recipe ledgers | 0 |

The protocol-upgrade ledger (2) varies in both lanes as well; it is never an entry.

Corpus entries whose order varies pin an order-normalised hash, and list every raw ordering seen (`change_order` in the [schema](/docs/corpus/schema)).

<Callout type="warn" title="For indexers">Never depend on the order of changes within an operation.</Callout>


# Replay (/docs/tools/replay)

**What it is.** Every corpus ledger fed to a real indexer, one at a time, through a mock of the RPC an indexer reads ledgers from, then a look at what the indexer stored.

**Why it matters.** An indexer that halts stops a wallet's history; one that stores a wrong balance is worse. Replay shows which ledgers do that before mainnet does.

```bash
make replay            # the whole corpus, then every sighting
make replay-main       # the corpus only
make replay-sightings  # #729/#716, #731, #745, #753 before and after
node replay/harness.mjs --adapter wallet-backend --target main \
  --entries muxed.payment.every-position
```

Needs Docker, Node ≥ 22.15 and the native reader (`make native`). Once the images and Go modules are cached nothing reaches the network: the ledgers come from the corpus. On a laptop under Docker, six sessions at a time, the full run takes about 9.5 minutes once the builds are cached.

Figure: how a replay works. A corpus ledger is served by a mock stellar-rpc to a real indexer build with its own database; what it did (its cursor, its process, the rows it stored) is compared with probes derived from the same ledger, which gives a verdict: handled, dropped, mishandled, stalled, crashed or halted.

![A terminal: the replay harness runs one protocol 22 ledger into wallet-backend main; three control ledgers are handled and the target is mishandled; a jq query over the harness's report lists the seven accounts stored short by their refunds.](https://xdrproof.dev/findings/f3-repro.gif)

## A session

One session replays one ledger, one distinct variant (its bytes and its network), into a fresh store.

<Steps>
<Step>

### Derive the probes

`replay/lib/derive.mjs` reads the ledger with rs-stellar-xdr and lists the **probes**: the facts a correct indexer has stored after ingesting it. They come from the ledger alone.

</Step>
<Step>

### Serve the ledger

`replay/lib/mock-rpc.mjs` serves the ledger as stellar-rpc v30.0.1 would: `getLedgers`, `getHealth`, `getLatestLedger`, `getNetwork`, `getVersionInfo`, and `getLedgerEntries` from the state the ledger leaves behind. Pagination, page limits and validation errors follow stellar-rpc word for word.

The mock knows only what the ledger states, so it knows less than stellar-rpc in three ways, each recorded per session: a method it does not serve, or a request such as a history-archive fetch, is refused; a ledger entry the ledger does not touch is answered "not found", though on a real network it may exist; and a contract entry whose TTL the ledger leaves untouched is served without `liveUntilLedgerSeq`. A verdict other than `handled` in a session that read such state is flagged and traced in the indexer's code before it is recorded.

</Step>
<Step>

### Prepare, start and watch

The adapter gives the indexer a clean store whose cursor sits just before the ledger and starts it against the mock. The harness polls the cursor until it passes the ledger, the process exits, the cursor stops moving, or the attempt times out. Once the ledger is passed, the process must still be running a second later. If the ledger was not passed, the indexer is started once more on the same store.

</Step>
<Step>

### Observe

The adapter answers every probe from what the indexer stored, and the harness compares.

</Step>
</Steps>

Before any session counts, the harness replays the **controls**: the plainest ledger of each protocol the target can decode. Each must get past its ledger, or the run stops as a setup failure.

## Verdicts

| Verdict | Rule |
|---|---|
| `handled` | the cursor passed the ledger and every applicable probe matches |
| `dropped` | the cursor passed, and a fact the ledger states is not stored |
| `mishandled` | the cursor passed, and a stored value differs from the ledger, or an invariant fails |
| `stalled` | the first attempt stopped making progress on the ledger without exiting; the restart got past it |
| `crashed` | the first attempt exited on the ledger; the restart got past it |
| `halted` | neither attempt passed the ledger |
| `unsupported` | the ledger's protocol is newer than the target decodes, or its network is not supported |
| `error` | an adapter command failed; never a finding (the run exits 2) |

## Probes

Each probe names a fact by its key and states the expected value in a canonical form: strkeys, decimal strings, XDR enum names. A muxed `M…` account is named by its `G…` account.

| Probe | Expected |
|---|---|
| `tx.present`, `tx.result`, `tx.fee_charged`, `tx.operations`, `tx.inner_hash` | the transaction is stored, with its result code, fee charged, operation count and, for a fee bump, the inner hash |
| `tx.participant`, `op.participant` | the source and fee source are attributed to the transaction; each operation's source to its operation |
| `account.created`, `account.removed`, `contract.created` | the accounts and contract instances the transaction created or removed are recorded |
| `signer.added`, `signer.updated`, `signer.removed` | the signer change is recorded, with its new weight |
| `trustline.added`, `trustline.removed` | the trustline the transaction created or removed is recorded |
| `balance.native`, `balance.trustline` | the balance at the end of the ledger, where the ledger changes it |

Two **invariants** cover everything the indexer stored in the session: `addresses.valid` (every stored address decodes and is one the ledger names) and `facts.extra` (every stored creation, merge and trustline change is one the ledger states). Facts on which indexers differ on purpose are not asserted.

## Bring your own indexer

The indexer is reached only through an **adapter**: a directory under `replay/adapters/` with an `adapter.toml` and a few shell commands (`prepare`, `start` and `cursor` are required; `observe`, `setup`, `stop`, `finish` and `teardown` are optional). Any indexer that reads `getLedgers` can be tested the same way. An adapter that implements only the three required commands still gets `handled`, `crashed` and `halted` for every ledger. The full contract is in [replay/README.md](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/replay/README.md).

The wallet-backend adapter builds each commit in a pinned Go image, runs TimescaleDB 2.28.2 as its compose file does, copies each session's database from a migrated template, runs `wallet-backend ingest` in live mode against the mock, and answers probes with one read of the session database.

<Callout title="A new failure, a changed one and a fixed one all fail the run">`replay/expectations/<adapter>@<target>.json` lists every variant that is not `handled`, with the exact probes that failed, the cause and the upstream issue. It also pins the set of variants judged (their count and a sha256 of their ids), so none can drop out of a run unnoticed.</Callout>


# Verify (/docs/tools/verify)

**What it is.** The basic check: every entry is exactly what it says it is, byte for byte, and every expected fact holds.

**Why it matters.** If the corpus were wrong, every test built on it would be wrong too. This runs in seconds, so it runs on every change.

```bash
make verify
# runs, with node: tools/strkey.test.mjs, tools/verify.mjs,
# tools/mined-verify.mjs and tools/auth-payload-check.mjs
node tools/verify.mjs --write   # also rewrite manifest.json
```

A real run of `make verify`, recorded 24 Nov 2026:

```text
 XDRPROOF   verify  · 263 entries · 634 ledger variants

  ╭─ Second reader · stellar-xdr-json ────────────────── 621/634─╮
  │ ! refuses very deep auth trees                           #67 │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ╭─ Corpus ──────────────────────────────────────────── 634/634─╮
  │ ✓ entries match the schema and the hazard list           263 │
  │ ✓ files match their sha256 and size                      634 │
  │ ✓ ledgers read back byte for byte                        634 │
  │ ✓ every focus transaction is in its ledger               634 │
  │ ✓ expected values hold                                 1,715 │
  │ ✓ ledgers with shuffled change order match                88 │
  │ ✓ manifest.json is up to date                                │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ╭─ Mined pubnet ledgers ──────────────────────────────── 37/37─╮
  │ ✓ 47 records and 223 values match the ledgers                │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ╭─ Keys and signatures ───────────────────────────────── 39/39─╮
  │ ✓ strkeys: 10 valid accepted, 19 invalid refused          29 │
  │ ✓ auth signatures hold (H-B16)                            10 │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

 PASSED   The corpus is intact.   12s

  every refused ledger and the hazards:  make verify DETAILS=1
```

## What it checks

<Steps>
<Step>

### Strkeys

Every SEP-0023 test vector must decode and re-encode (valid), or be rejected (invalid). This covers XDRProof's own strkey codec, which the schema walker uses.

</Step>
<Step>

### The entry

The entry is validated against `schema/v1/entry.schema.json` (ajv, strict mode). Its `id` must match its directory, and every hazard id must exist in the registry. Variant keys must be unique, and each file name must start with its key.

</Step>
<Step>

### The bytes and the round trip

Size and sha256 must match; `.zst` variants are checked on their decompressed bytes. The **native reader** (rs-stellar-xdr 30.0.0, depth limit 1500) decodes the bytes, renders SEP-0051 JSON and encodes them again. The result must be identical, byte for byte.

</Step>
<Step>

### The focus and the facts

The focus transaction hash must be in the ledger, as an outer or fee-bump inner hash. Every fact that applies to the variant must hold at its JSON Pointer path. If the entry's change order is unstable, the order-normalised hash must match, and the shipped bytes must be one of the orderings seen.

</Step>
<Step>

### A second reader

The WASM build `@stellar/stellar-xdr-json` 30.0.0 decodes each variant again, with no fallback. If it renders different JSON, the run fails. If it cannot decode a variant at all (for example at its depth limit), verify lists it and records `fails` in the manifest, and the run still passes. Today 621 of 634 variants agree.

</Step>
<Step>

### The manifest

`manifest.json` is rebuilt from the entries. Without `--write`, verify fails if the committed file has drifted.

</Step>
<Step>

### The mined ledgers

`tools/mined-verify.mjs` checks every [mined ledger](/docs/corpus/mined). It must match its hash and size, round-trip through the native reader, and carry the recorded sequence and protocol. Every finding's transaction and JSON path must be present.

</Step>
<Step>

### The create-contract authorization payload

For the two v1 create-contract entries, `tools/auth-payload-check.mjs` encodes each authorization preimage by hand twice, once as the entry's own bytes and once as the V2 rendering the host hashes, and verifies the ed25519 signature against both. The entry stellar-core accepted verifies only as V2; the one signed over its own bytes verifies only as v1, and core failed it. No SDK or host code is involved. See hazard [H-B16](/docs/hazards/layer-b#h-b16).

</Step>
</Steps>

## Output

A table with one row per variant: entry@variant, protocol, source, round trip, facts, WASM reader. Then a summary of the counts (entries, variants, hazards targeted), an `OK` line, and the mined-ledger report.


# Use it on your code (/docs/use)

**What it is.** The rest of these docs show how XDRProof tests other people's code. This section is for your team: the shortest way to point XDRProof at your own SDK, your own Go indexer and your own indexer.

**Why it matters.** The corpus holds the rare ledgers that broke real indexers and SDKs. Running it in your own CI means your code meets them before your users do, and keeps meeting them on every change.
- [Test your SDK](https://xdrproof.dev/docs/use/sdk): A copy-paste test in JavaScript, Go, Rust or Python, with nothing to clone: every corpus ledger must decode and re-encode to the same bytes.
- [Lint your Go indexer](https://xdrproof.dev/docs/use/lint): Run xplint on your repository for the three ingestion mistakes, with SARIF for GitHub code scanning.
- [Replay your indexer](https://xdrproof.dev/docs/use/replay): Write a small adapter and replay every corpus ledger into your indexer, with a verdict for each from what it stored.

Nothing to clone for the first two: the SDK test fetches the pinned corpus from GitHub and checks every file's sha256, and the linter runs straight from its Go module path. Replaying an indexer runs the harness from a clone today.

Every snippet in this section was run in an empty folder on 19 November 2026. The output shown is what it printed. Where something did not work as first written, the page says so.


# Lint your Go indexer (/docs/use/lint)

**What it is.** `xplint` reads your Go indexer's source and points at the exact lines that make one of three mistakes. You run it on your own repository with one command; there is nothing to install first.

**Why it matters.** These three mistakes are how real indexers have halted or stored wrong data. Finding them in review costs a minute; finding them after a ledger arrives costs an incident.

## The three mistakes, in plain words

| Rule | The mistake | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| **XP001** | Trusting a field stellar-core does not check. Memo text, contract strings and muxed addresses are whatever the sender put there. | Validate the bytes (UTF-8, length), and switch on an address's kind before treating it as an account. |
| **XP002** | Walking a nested structure with no limit. Authorization trees and nested contract values can be hundreds of levels deep. | Carry a depth and a node budget, and at the limit stop descending. Never fail the ledger: it fails again on every retry. |
| **XP003** | Taking participants from the envelope. The envelope says what a transaction asked for; the meta says what happened. | Attribute accounts from the meta, and only for transactions that succeeded. |

Each rule has sub-rules with stable IDs; the full list, with the evidence behind each, is on [Linter](/docs/tools/linter#the-three-mistakes).

## Run it

From your repository's root, with Go 1.26 or later and the same cgo setup your packages build with:

```bash
go run github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/linter/cmd/xplint@latest ./...
```

Go fetches the linter's module straight from GitHub (`github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/linter`); nothing is cloned or installed. It needs no module of its own either: run from an empty folder, `go run github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/linter/cmd/xplint@latest -list` printed every rule. Run from an empty folder on a fresh clone of [stellar/wallet-backend](https://github.com/stellar/wallet-backend) at `18db88f`, in the `golang:1.27` image with an empty module cache, it printed:

```text
internal/indexer/processors/contract_deploy.go:116:2: XP002/walk-unbudgeted: closure walkInvocation recurses over SorobanAuthorizedInvocation with no depth or node budget
internal/services/blend/processor.go:387:21: XP001/muxed-as-account: an address that may be muxed (M...) or not an account is passed to stageHistoryRow, where it reaches .WithAccount() at blend/processor.go:439; it comes from ScAddress.String at blend/scval.go:71
internal/services/blend/processor.go:579:16: XP001/muxed-as-account: an address that may be muxed (M...) or not an account is passed to routeEntry, where it reaches a map key at blend/processor.go:819; it comes from ScAddress.String at blend/scval.go:71
internal/services/blend/scval.go:182:6: XP001/muxed-as-account: an address that may be muxed (M...) or not an account reaches a map key; it comes from ScAddress.String at blend/scval.go:71
exit status 1
```

Each line is `file:line:col: RULE: message`. The exit status is 0 with no findings, 1 with findings, and 2 when the packages could not be loaded. All four of these are real; what each one means, and the patches that clear them, are on [Linter](/docs/tools/linter#wallet-backend-main).

## In CI: SARIF for GitHub code scanning

```bash
go run github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/linter/cmd/xplint@latest \
  -format sarif -o xplint.sarif ./...
```

The same run wrote the same four findings as SARIF 2.1.0:

```text
      3 "ruleId": "XP001/muxed-as-account"
      1 "ruleId": "XP002/walk-unbudgeted"
```

Upload `xplint.sarif` with GitHub's `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif` and each finding appears on its line in pull requests. Other flags: `-format json`, `-rules XP002,XP003/declared-auth` for a subset, and `-list` for every rule.

<Callout title="What it does not see">
xplint follows Go values through SSA within and across your packages. It does not follow calls through interfaces or function values, values sent over channels, or flows through a database, and it knows the go-stellar-sdk's accessors, not your own XDR types. A clean run means none of the patterns it knows, not no bugs. [Limits](/docs/tools/linter#limits)
</Callout>


# Replay your indexer (/docs/use/replay)

**What it is.** A way to feed every rare ledger in the corpus into your own indexer, the way an RPC would serve it, and get a verdict for each one: handled, dropped, mishandled, stalled, crashed or halted.

**Why it matters.** It is the closest thing to meeting those ledgers in production, without waiting for them. The verdict comes from your indexer's own state, so a wrong balance is caught even when nothing crashes.

Figure: how a replay works. A corpus ledger is served by a mock stellar-rpc to a real indexer build with its own database; what it did (its cursor, its process, the rows it stored) is compared with probes derived from the same ledger, which gives a verdict: handled, dropped, mishandled, stalled, crashed or halted.

## Try it on wallet-backend first

The replay harness runs from the repository today, so this one needs a clone, with Docker and Node 22.15 or later. The planned `xdrproof` command-line tool (Tranche 1, by 2 February 2027) brings `xdrproof replay` without one.

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof && cd xdrproof
make tools/node_modules native
node replay/harness.mjs --adapter wallet-backend --target main \
  --entries muxed.payment.every-position
```

What it printed on 19 November 2026, in 113 seconds with the Docker images already cached (a cold build downloads Go modules first; the adapter allows 20 minutes):

```text
wallet-backend@main (18db88f4ba48, protocol_max 30): 2 variants, 2 sessions, 0 unsupported
  3/3 sessions
  control executable-ref.invoke@p28-mainnet-generated: handled
  control failure.path-payment-strict-send.no-destination-mainnet@p29-mainnet-mined-l65517499: handled
  control event.classic.payment-transfer@p30-mainnet-generated: handled
  2/2 sessions

handled 2   (…/replay/runs/wallet-backend@main/report.json; harness peak RSS 79 MiB)
  the indexer read ledger entries the corpus does not hold: contract_data x4 (answered not found)
partial run (2 variants judged): each matches its expectation; the judged-set check needs a full run.
OK: every verdict matches replay/expectations/wallet-backend@main.json.
```

The control ledgers run first: the plainest ledger of each protocol the target decodes, each of which must get through before any session counts. The `contract_data` line is the mock telling you the indexer asked for state the ledger does not hold (wallet-backend reads two Blend contracts at startup); a verdict that depends on such a read is flagged and traced by hand. Drop `--entries` to replay the whole corpus.

## Write an adapter for your indexer

An adapter is a folder under `replay/adapters/` with an `adapter.toml` and a few commands. Any indexer that reads ledgers through `getLedgers` can join. Below is a starting template, cut down from wallet-backend's adapter; fill in your own commands.

```toml title="replay/adapters/your-indexer/adapter.toml"
schema = "xdrproof.adapter/v1"
name   = "your-indexer"

[delivery]
kind = "rpc"   # ledgers come through a mock stellar-rpc

[supports]
networks = ["pubnet", "testnet"]
# the probe kinds your observe command answers
probes   = ["tx.present", "balance.native"]

[targets.main]
ref = "<commit>"      # the commit to build
protocol_max = 30     # the newest protocol its decoder reads

[commands]                  # run from the adapter folder
prepare = "./prepare.sh"    # a clean store, cursor before the ledger
start   = "./start.sh"      # the indexer, pointed at XDRPROOF_RPC_URL
cursor  = "./cursor.sh"     # print the last ledger committed
observe = "node observe.mjs" # optional: answer probes, read-only

[timeouts]
setup_s = 1200
ledger_s = 30
session_s = 120

[limits]
memory_mb = 1024
```

| Command | Required | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `setup` | no | once per target: build the commit, start the store |
| `prepare` | yes | per session: a clean store with the cursor just before the ledger |
| `start` | yes | per session: run the indexer in the foreground against the mock RPC |
| `cursor` | yes | print the last ledger the indexer committed |
| `observe` | no | read `{"probes": [...]}` on stdin and answer each one `present` (with the stored value) or `absent`, read-only |
| `stop`, `finish`, `teardown` | no | stop the indexer, drop the session's store, clean up |

Each command gets the session in its environment: `XDRPROOF_FIRST_LEDGER`, `XDRPROOF_LAST_LEDGER`, `XDRPROOF_NETWORK_PASSPHRASE`, `XDRPROOF_RPC_URL` (and a `_DOCKER` form that reaches the host from a container), `XDRPROOF_TARGET_REF` and more; the full list is in [`replay/README.md`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/blob/main/replay/README.md#adapter-contract).

With only `prepare`, `start` and `cursor`, every ledger already gets `handled`, `crashed` or `halted`. Add `observe` and the harness can also tell `dropped` and `mishandled`: it works out probes from the ledger's own meta (transactions, participants, signers, trustlines, balances, contracts) and asks your store about each one.

The worked example is [`replay/adapters/wallet-backend/`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/tree/main/replay/adapters/wallet-backend): it builds each commit in a pinned Go image, runs TimescaleDB as wallet-backend's compose file does, copies each session's database from a migrated template, and answers every probe with one read of the session database. Its `cursor.sh` is one SQL query.

## What a verdict means

Each ledger gets two attempts: if the first does not get past it, the indexer is restarted once on the same store.

| Verdict | Means |
|---|---|
| `handled` | the cursor passed the ledger and every probe your adapter answers matches it |
| `dropped` | the cursor passed, and something the ledger states is not stored |
| `mishandled` | the cursor passed, and a stored value differs from the ledger, or an invariant fails |
| `stalled` | the first attempt stopped making progress without exiting; the restart got past the ledger |
| `crashed` | the first attempt exited on the ledger; the restart got past it |
| `halted` | neither attempt got past the ledger: ingestion is stuck |

Two more statuses are not findings: `unsupported` (the ledger's protocol is newer than your target decodes, or its network is not supported) and `error` (an adapter command failed; the run exits 2).

See [Replay](/docs/tools/replay) for how sessions, probes and expectations work, and for wallet-backend's results across the whole corpus.


# Test your SDK (/docs/use/sdk)

**What it is.** One test file for your SDK's test suite. It fetches every ledger in the corpus at a pinned commit, checks each one's sha256, decodes it as `LedgerCloseMeta`, encodes it again, and checks that the bytes are identical.

**Why it matters.** A ledger that does not round-trip is a ledger your SDK reads wrongly: a field dropped, a value changed, or a shape it cannot read at all. The corpus is the rarest valid ledgers stellar-core writes, so this is the cheapest way to meet them in CI before a user does.

<Steps>
<Step>

### Nothing to clone

The test reads `manifest.json` from GitHub at a pinned commit, then each ledger it lists from `raw.githubusercontent.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/<commit>/entries/<id>/<file>`, and checks every file against the sha256 the manifest records. It keeps what it fetched in `.xdrproof/`, so later runs read from disk: cache that folder in CI, and add it to `.gitignore`. To move to a newer corpus, change the commit.

The manifest lists 634 ledgers. The 37 mined from the public data lake ship zstd-compressed (`.xdr.zst`); the test decompresses them, and the recorded sha256 is of the ledger itself.

**Prefer a pinned copy in your repository?** Add it as a git submodule and point the test's cache folder at it (`CACHE = "xdrproof"`); it then reads the files in place and fetches nothing.

```bash
git submodule add https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof xdrproof
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Add the test

<Tabs items={["JavaScript", "Go", "Rust", "Python"]}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">

`@stellar/stellar-sdk` 17.4.0. Node 22.15 or later, for its built-in `fetch` and zstd.

```js title="xdrproof.test.mjs"
// Every corpus ledger must decode and re-encode to the same bytes.
// Fetches the pinned corpus once into .xdrproof/, checking sha256.
// Run: node --test   (Node 22.15 or later)
import { test } from "node:test"
import assert from "node:assert/strict"
import { createHash } from "node:crypto"
import {
  existsSync, mkdirSync, readFileSync, writeFileSync,
} from "node:fs"
import { dirname, join } from "node:path"
import { zstdDecompressSync } from "node:zlib"
import { xdr } from "@stellar/stellar-sdk"

const PIN = "24810e7256fcf8da5d5cc6e0a8422b7c110820d0"
const RAW =
  `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/${PIN}/`
const CACHE = join(".xdrproof", PIN)

async function get(path) {
  const file = join(CACHE, path)
  if (!existsSync(file)) {
    const res = await fetch(RAW + path)
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${res.status} ${path}`)
    mkdirSync(dirname(file), { recursive: true })
    writeFileSync(file, Buffer.from(await res.arrayBuffer()))
  }
  return readFileSync(file)
}

const { rows } = JSON.parse(await get("manifest.json"))
// fetch the corpus 8 files at a time before the tests start
for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i += 8)
  await Promise.all(rows.slice(i, i + 8).map((r) => get(r.file)))
for (const row of rows) {
  test(row.entry_id, async () => {
    let bytes = await get(row.file)
    // mined ledgers ship zstd-compressed; sha256 is of the ledger
    if (row.file.endsWith(".zst")) bytes = zstdDecompressSync(bytes)
    const sha = createHash("sha256").update(bytes).digest("hex")
    assert.equal(sha, row.sha256, "not the pinned bytes")
    const meta = xdr.LedgerCloseMeta.fromXDR(bytes)
    assert.ok(Buffer.from(meta.toXDR()).equals(bytes), "bytes differ")
  })
}
```

```bash
npm install @stellar/stellar-sdk@17.4.0
node --test xdrproof.test.mjs
```

From an empty folder, on Node 25.9, the first run (fetching the corpus) took 56 seconds; the second, from `.xdrproof/`, 3.5 seconds. The end of the run:

```text
ℹ suites 0
ℹ pass 634
ℹ fail 0
```

<Tab value="Go">

`github.com/stellar/go-stellar-sdk` v0.9.0. `xdr.SafeUnmarshal` keeps the SDK's default depth limit.

```go title="xdrproof_test.go"
// Every corpus ledger must decode and re-encode to the same bytes.
// Fetches the pinned corpus once into .xdrproof/, checking sha256.
// Run: go test ./...
package xdrproof_test

import (
	"bytes"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"encoding/hex"
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"net/http"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"github.com/klauspost/compress/zstd"
	"github.com/stellar/go-stellar-sdk/xdr"
)

const pin = "24810e7256fcf8da5d5cc6e0a8422b7c110820d0"
const raw = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/" +
	pin + "/"

func get(path string) ([]byte, error) {
	file := filepath.Join(".xdrproof", pin, path)
	if b, err := os.ReadFile(file); err == nil {
		return b, nil
	}
	res, err := http.Get(raw + path)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	defer res.Body.Close()
	if res.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %s", path, res.Status)
	}
	b, err := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	os.MkdirAll(filepath.Dir(file), 0o755)
	return b, os.WriteFile(file, b, 0o644)
}

func TestCorpusRoundTrip(t *testing.T) {
	m, err := get("manifest.json")
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	var manifest struct {
		Rows []struct {
			ID     string `json:"entry_id"`
			File   string `json:"file"`
			Sha256 string `json:"sha256"`
		} `json:"rows"`
	}
	if err := json.Unmarshal(m, &manifest); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	unzst, _ := zstd.NewReader(nil)
	for _, row := range manifest.Rows {
		t.Run(row.ID, func(t *testing.T) {
			t.Parallel() // fetches run side by side
			b, err := get(row.File)
			if err != nil {
				t.Fatal(err)
			}
			// mined ledgers: zstd-compressed; sha256 is of the ledger
			if strings.HasSuffix(row.File, ".zst") {
				if b, err = unzst.DecodeAll(b, nil); err != nil {
					t.Fatal(err)
				}
			}
			sum := sha256.Sum256(b)
			if hex.EncodeToString(sum[:]) != row.Sha256 {
				t.Fatal("not the pinned bytes")
			}
			var meta xdr.LedgerCloseMeta
			if err := xdr.SafeUnmarshal(b, &meta); err != nil {
				t.Fatal("decode: ", err)
			}
			out, err := meta.MarshalBinary()
			if err != nil {
				t.Fatal("encode: ", err)
			}
			if !bytes.Equal(out, b) {
				t.Fatal("re-encoded bytes differ")
			}
		})
	}
}
```

```bash
go get github.com/stellar/go-stellar-sdk@v0.9.0
go mod tidy
go test ./...
```

`go mod tidy` is needed: `go get` on the SDK's root module leaves the `xdr` package's own dependencies out of `go.sum`, and a first try without it stopped with `missing go.sum entry`. From an empty folder, on Go 1.27.4:

```text
ok  	example.com/check	15.015s
```

`go test -v` lists 634 passing subtests, one per ledger, and no failures.

<Tab value="Rust">

`stellar-xdr` 30.0.0 has **no default depth limit**: you choose one in `Limits`. The deepest corpus ledgers need more than 500 levels (see [how deep is too deep](/docs/findings/reported)); 1500 reads them all.

```toml title="Cargo.toml"
[dev-dependencies]
stellar-xdr = "=30.0.0"
serde_json = "1"
sha2 = "0.10"
ureq = "2"
zstd = "0.13"
```

```rust title="tests/xdrproof.rs"
// Every corpus ledger must decode and re-encode to the same bytes.
// Fetches the pinned corpus once into .xdrproof/, checking sha256.
// Run: cargo test --release -- --nocapture
use sha2::{Digest, Sha256};
use std::{fs, io::Read, path::Path};
use stellar_xdr::{LedgerCloseMeta, Limits, ReadXdr, WriteXdr};

const PIN: &str = "24810e7256fcf8da5d5cc6e0a8422b7c110820d0";

fn get(path: &str) -> Vec<u8> {
    let file = Path::new(".xdrproof").join(PIN).join(path);
    if let Ok(b) = fs::read(&file) {
        return b;
    }
    let url = format!(
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/{}/{}",
        PIN, path
    );
    let mut b = Vec::new();
    let res = ureq::get(&url).call().unwrap();
    res.into_reader().read_to_end(&mut b).unwrap();
    fs::create_dir_all(file.parent().unwrap()).unwrap();
    fs::write(&file, &b).unwrap();
    b
}

// rs-stellar-xdr has no default depth limit: choose one.
// The deepest corpus ledgers need more than 500.
fn limits() -> Limits {
    Limits { depth: 1500, len: 256 * 1024 * 1024 }
}

#[test]
fn corpus_round_trips() {
    let m: serde_json::Value =
        serde_json::from_slice(&get("manifest.json")).unwrap();
    let rows = m["rows"].as_array().unwrap();
    // fetch the corpus 8 files at a time before the checks
    let files: Vec<&str> =
        rows.iter().map(|r| r["file"].as_str().unwrap()).collect();
    for chunk in files.chunks(8) {
        std::thread::scope(|s| {
            for f in chunk {
                s.spawn(move || get(f));
            }
        });
    }
    for row in rows {
        let id = row["entry_id"].as_str().unwrap();
        let file = row["file"].as_str().unwrap();
        let mut bytes = get(file);
        // mined ledgers ship zstd-compressed; sha256 is of the ledger
        if file.ends_with(".zst") {
            bytes = zstd::decode_all(&bytes[..]).unwrap();
        }
        let sha = format!("{:x}", Sha256::digest(&bytes));
        assert_eq!(sha, row["sha256"].as_str().unwrap(), "{id}");
        let meta = LedgerCloseMeta::from_xdr(&bytes, limits())
            .unwrap_or_else(|e| panic!("{id}: decode: {e}"));
        let out = meta.to_xdr(limits()).unwrap();
        assert_eq!(out, bytes, "{id}: bytes differ");
    }
    println!("{} corpus variants round-trip", rows.len());
}
```

```bash
cargo test --release -- --nocapture
```

The types are at the crate root in 30.0.0 (a first try with `stellar_xdr::curr::…` did not compile). From an empty folder, on cargo 1.98.1:


<Tab value="Python">

`stellar-sdk` 17.0.1 (py-stellar-base), with `zstandard` for the mined ledgers.

```python title="test_xdrproof.py"
# Every corpus ledger must decode and re-encode to the same bytes.
# Fetches the pinned corpus once into .xdrproof/, checking sha256.
# Run: pytest -q
import hashlib
import json
import pathlib
import urllib.request
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

import pytest
import zstandard
from stellar_sdk import xdr

PIN = "24810e7256fcf8da5d5cc6e0a8422b7c110820d0"
RAW = f"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/{PIN}/"
CACHE = pathlib.Path(".xdrproof") / PIN


def get(path):
    file = CACHE / path
    if not file.exists():
        file.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with urllib.request.urlopen(RAW + path) as res:
            file.write_bytes(res.read())
    return file.read_bytes()


ROWS = json.loads(get("manifest.json"))["rows"]
# fetch the corpus 8 files at a time before the tests start
with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as pool:
    list(pool.map(get, [row["file"] for row in ROWS]))
IDS = [row["entry_id"] for row in ROWS]


@pytest.mark.parametrize("row", ROWS, ids=IDS)
def test_round_trip(row):
    data = get(row["file"])
    # mined ledgers ship zstd-compressed; sha256 is of the ledger
    if row["file"].endswith(".zst"):
        unzst = zstandard.ZstdDecompressor().decompressobj()
        data = unzst.decompress(data)
    assert hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() == row["sha256"]
    meta = xdr.LedgerCloseMeta.from_xdr_bytes(data)
    assert meta.to_xdr_bytes() == data
```



<Step>

### Go further

A byte round trip is the floor. Each entry also lists the **facts** a correct reader must find (`expected.facts` in its `entry.json`, at a JSON Pointer path in the SEP-0051 rendering), and some list SDK checks (`expected.sdk_checks`). [Conformance](/docs/tools/conformance) runs all of them, through the same bytes, in every build.

</Step>
</Steps>

<Callout title="Depth">
The deepest valid ledgers in the corpus need more than 500 levels of XDR nesting. js-stellar-sdk 17.4.0, go-stellar-sdk v0.9.0 and py-stellar-base 17.0.1 read all of them with their defaults. rs-stellar-xdr has no default, so pick a limit (1500 above). `@stellar/stellar-xdr-json` 30.0.0 refuses 13 of them: [F-1](/docs/findings/reported).
</Callout>

## Join the matrix

[Conformance](/docs/tools/conformance) runs 6 SDK builds over the whole corpus today (JavaScript, WebAssembly, Rust, Go and two Python packages), plus 5 older releases on the fixed-bug regressions. Any SDK can join by wrapping itself in a **testee**: a small program that reads one JSON request per line on stdin and writes one JSON answer per line on stdout.

| `op` | Input | Answer when `ok` |
|---|---|---|
| `hello` | none | `implementation: {sdk, package, version, runtime}`, `ops: [...]` |
| `decode` | `{type, xdr}`: a type name as rs-stellar-xdr spells it, and base64 bytes | `xdr`: your re-encoding; `json`: your SEP-0051 rendering, if you have one |
| `encode_json` | `{type, json}` | `xdr`: base64 |
| `strkey_decode` | `{strkey}` | `kind`: the first letter; `payload`: hex of the bytes between version byte and checksum |
| `native` | `{type: "ScVal", xdr}` | `value`: your native projection, rendered losslessly |

Every answer carries `status`: `ok`, `error` (with the stage and message) or `unsupported`. Anything your SDK cannot do is `unsupported`, recorded as not applicable, never as a failure. The six testees in [`conformance/testees/`](https://github.com/XDRProof/xdrproof/tree/main/conformance/testees) are working examples, from 28 to 118 lines each.

The Java, Swift, Dart, PHP and .NET SDKs are not run today. Testees for all five, run over the whole corpus with every difference pinned, are Deliverable 10 of the grant's Tranche 3 ([Architecture](/docs/start/architecture)).
